# Burds Family Practice

> Independent family medicine clinic in Peosta, Iowa, serving Dubuque and western Dubuque County. Primary care for all ages, same-day sick visits, Direct Primary Care from $99/month, DOT/CDL and occupational health physicals, and mental health care for ages 12 and up. Accepting new patients: call (563) 588-6659.

## Key facts

- Name: Burds Family Practice (Burds Family Practice, PLLC), an independent, locally owned family medicine clinic. Not part of a hospital system.
- Address: 8411 Peosta Commercial Ct, Suite 8, Peosta, IA 52068 (just off U.S. Highway 20 between Dubuque and Dyersville, western Dubuque County, Iowa)
- Phone: (563) 588-6659 · Email: bfpstaff@burdsfamilypractice.com
- Hours: Monday–Wednesday 8 AM–5 PM, Thursday 8 AM–6 PM, Friday 8 AM–12 PM, closed Saturday and Sunday
- Accepting new patients of all ages, newborns through seniors. Same-day sick visits available by phone.
- Insurance: most major insurance plans accepted. Direct Primary Care (DPC) membership also available: $99/month adult, $79/month spouse or partner, $49/month child, $276/month family of four; unlimited visits, $0 copays, same- or next-day access, direct phone and text access to your provider.
- Providers: Jennifer (Jenny) Burds, DNP, ARNP (owner, family nurse practitioner, FMCSA National Registry certified medical examiner for DOT/CDL physicals); Channah Chase, DNP, FNP-BC (family nurse practitioner); Jenna Hefel, DNP, PMHNP-BC (psychiatric nurse practitioner, ages 12+, certified in perinatal mental health).
- Services: primary care, wellness exams, sick visits, pediatrics and well-child checks, school and sports physicals, chronic disease management, immunizations, in-office labs, joint injections, mental health care, DOT/CDL physicals, pre-employment physicals, 12-panel drug screening, work injury care, infrared sauna, and medical aesthetics through sister medspa SkinRx by Burds (burdsskinrx.com).
- Serves: Peosta, Dubuque, Asbury, Epworth, Farley, Dyersville, Cascade, Bernard, Centralia, Graf, Holy Cross, Sherrill and the rest of Dubuque County, Iowa.
- Ratings: 5.0 stars on Google (100+ reviews), Facebook and Tebra.
- Founded 2022 (PLLC formed September 16, 2022), clinic opened 2023. Organization NPI 1194432864.
- Patient portal: https://portal.kareo.com/pp-webapp/app/new/login
- In an emergency, call 911.

# About Us & Our Nurse Practitioners | Peosta, IA

URL: https://www.burdsfamilypractice.com/about.html

Our Story · Peosta, Iowa

## Personalized health care in your community

Burds Family Practice helps patients and families feel their best so they can do what they love. We take the time to listen, find root causes, and provide thoughtful care for every stage of life, from newborns to seniors.

Meet the Team
Our Local Favorites

A Note From Jenny

### Doing what I love, in the town I love

Healthcare has been Jenny Burds' calling her entire career. Opening an independent practice in Peosta let her care for neighbors in the place that means the most to her. The Burds family was among Peosta's founding families, and she is proud to be part of the town's growth.

Community runs through the entire clinic: local builders shaped our suite, local artists' work hangs on our walls, and we partner with local vendors and fellow small businesses whenever we can.

Founded September 2022 · Opened 2023 · Peosta, Iowa

Burds Family Practice, PLLC · Org NPI 1194432864
Facebook · 1.9K Followers →

Rooted in Peosta

### The compass, the leaves, and the roots

Our emblem pairs a compass star with leaves reaching upward and roots anchored deep below. That reflects how we practice: guiding families through health decisions while staying grounded in the Peosta community we grew up in.

We also invest outside our walls, serving as a Platinum Sponsor of the 'Be A Light' 5K Mental Health Awareness Fun Run and supporting local youth and wellness programs across western Dubuque County.

Our Team

### Providers who know your name

You see the same trusted faces at every visit, backed by decades of family medicine, mental health, and clinic experience.

#### Jenny Burds, DNP, ARNP

Family Nurse Practitioner · Owner

With 30 years in healthcare, including more than 15 years as a nurse practitioner and a Doctorate from Clarke University, Jenny founded Burds Family Practice (Individual NPI 1639433030) to bring unhurried family care home to Peosta. She is also an FMCSA National Registry Certified Medical Examiner for DOT physicals. Outside the clinic, she loves workout classes and traveling.
Tebra Profile & Reviews

#### Channah Chase, DNP, FNP-BC

Family Nurse Practitioner

Channah earned her Doctor of Nursing Practice at Clarke University and brings more than 8 years of nursing experience caring for patients of every age. She and her daughter love the outdoors and spend as much free time as possible on the river.
Tebra Care Profile

#### Jenna Hefel, DNP, PMHNP-BC

Psychiatric Mental Health Nurse Practitioner

Board-certified and practicing in psychiatry since 2015, Jenna provides psychiatric evaluations and medication management for patients ages 12 and up and holds a Perinatal Mental Health Certification. She grew up near Cascade and lives on a small farm with her family.
Tebra Care Profile

#### Allie Morris, CMA

Certified Medical Assistant · Clinic Manager

Allie has been part of the clinic since opening day. A graduate of NICC's medical assistant program, she rooms patients, draws labs, gives immunizations, coordinates patient calls and results, and keeps daily clinic operations running smoothly.

#### Trish Hohnecker

Director of Revenue Cycle

Trish brings more than 30 years of medical billing, coding, and insurance expertise to ensure your billing and financial experience is straightforward. She also served 15 years as a volunteer paramedic with Centralia Peosta EMS/Fire.

“Healthcare should feel like a relationship, not a transaction.”
Jenny Burds, DNP · Founder, Burds Family Practice

Areas We Serve

## A family clinic close to home for all of western Dubuque County

Burds Family Practice sits just off U.S. Highway 20 in Peosta, Iowa, between Dubuque and Dyersville. Families drive in from across the county because they get unhurried visits, the same providers every time, and same-day sick appointments without the hassle of a big hospital system.

Call (563) 588-6659
Get Directions

Communities

### Where our patients come from

You don't need to live in Peosta to be our patient. Anyone can establish care with us, whether you have insurance or choose our Direct Primary Care membership.

#### Peosta

Our home town. The clinic is at 8411 Peosta Commercial Ct, Suite 8, in the commercial park off U.S. 20. Founder Jenny Burds's family was among Peosta's founding families.

#### Dubuque & Asbury

A straight shot west on U.S. 20. Dubuque and Asbury families choose us for an independent, small-practice feel, with providers who know them by name.

#### Epworth & Farley

Just down U.S. 20. We're a convenient choice for school and sports physicals, well-child checks and same-day sick visits for Western Dubuque students and families.

#### Dyersville

Head east on U.S. 20 to Peosta. Dyersville-area drivers and employers can get DOT/CDL physicals, pre-employment exams and drug screens here with same-week scheduling.

#### Cascade & Bernard

South-county families come to us for whole-household care, from newborn checkups to Medicare-age wellness visits, all with one familiar care team.

#### Centralia, Graf, Holy Cross & Sherrill

Smaller towns across the county are part of our patient family too. Our Direct Primary Care members can reach their provider by phone or text instead of driving in for every question.

Why make the drive

Common questions

### Coming to us from out of town

**Q: Do I have to live in Peosta to be a patient?**

No. We welcome patients from Dubuque, Asbury, Epworth, Farley, Dyersville, Cascade and anywhere else. Call (563) 588-6659 to establish care.

**Q: Is there a family doctor near Dubuque accepting new patients?**

Yes. Burds Family Practice in Peosta, just west of Dubuque on U.S. 20, is accepting new patients of all ages, from newborns to seniors.

**Q: Where can I get a DOT physical near Dubuque or Dyersville?**

At our Peosta clinic. Jenny Burds, DNP, ARNP is a certified medical examiner on the FMCSA National Registry, and we offer same-week DOT/CDL physicals and drug screens.

**Q: Is Direct Primary Care available in Dubuque County?**

Yes. We offer Direct Primary Care memberships for $99/month per adult, $79/month for a spouse or partner and $49/month per child, with unlimited visits and $0 copays.

**Q: Where do I park?**

There's easy parking right outside our suite at 8411 Peosta Commercial Ct.

Call our Peosta office and our team will help you get started, wherever in Dubuque County you call home.

## Primary care for one simple monthly fee

Direct Primary Care is a simple membership for your everyday health. One monthly fee covers unlimited primary care visits, $0 copays, same- or next-day scheduling, and direct access to your provider without insurance hassles.

What's Included

### Everything your everyday health needs

Instead of billing insurance every time you walk through the door, your membership keeps your care team on your side whenever something comes up.

- Unlimited primary care visits with $0 per-visit copays

- Same- or next-day appointments with unhurried time

- Direct access to your provider by phone, text, or telehealth

- Annual wellness exams, school physicals, and sports physicals

- Chronic condition management (diabetes, hypertension, thyroid, asthma)

- Prescription management and coordinated referrals when needed

Is DPC Right for You?

### Who gets the most value from DPC

#### Self-employed & small businesses

Predictable monthly care for owners, freelancers, and employees without high-cost group plans.

#### High-deductible plan holders

Pair a lower-premium catastrophic plan with DPC so everyday visits never eat into a $5,000 deductible.

#### Busy families

When kids spike a fever or need a sports physical, you call and get seen without worrying about another copay.

#### Chronic condition management

Check in as often as needed for blood pressure, diabetes, or thyroid adjustments with $0 visit fees.

#### Prevention-minded patients

Never hesitate to ask a question early before a small concern becomes an urgent trip.

#### Anyone tired of rushed care

Real relationships with providers who know your name and never push you out in ten minutes.

Common Questions

### DPC questions, answered

**Q: Do I still need health insurance?**

DPC covers your everyday primary care, not hospital stays, surgeries, ER visits, or specialist imaging. Most members pair DPC with a high-deductible or catastrophic health plan (or health-share) so they're protected for major events while paying less overall.

**Q: How much does DPC cost?**

Membership is $99/month for a single adult, $79/month for a spouse or partner, and $49/month per child ($276/month for a family of four). Call (563) 588-6659 to verify current enrollment options for your household.

**Q: Can I use my HSA or FSA?**

In many cases, yes. Eligibility depends on your plan administrator and federal rules, so check with your HSA/FSA provider.

**Q: What if I need a specialist or hospitalization?**

We refer you to trusted local specialists, transfer your history, and stay actively involved as your advocate and care coordinator.

**Q: Can kids and seniors join?**

Yes. We care for patients from newborns through seniors, and families of every shape can enroll together.

### Ready to try simpler, personal care?

Call us to walk through the numbers and see whether DPC or insurance-based care fits your family best.

Areas We Serve

Quick answers

### Questions families ask us most

**Q: Is Burds Family Practice accepting new patients?**

Yes. We're accepting new patients of every age, from newborns to seniors. Call (563) 588-6659 to schedule, or read our new patient guide.

**Q: Can I be seen today if I'm sick?**

Usually, yes. We hold same-day appointments for illnesses, infections and minor injuries. Call us when we open at 8 AM and we'll find you a time. For a medical emergency, call 911.

**Q: Where is the clinic and what are your hours?**

We're at 8411 Peosta Commercial Ct, Suite 8, Peosta, IA 52068, just off U.S. Highway 20 near Dubuque. Hours are Monday–Wednesday 8 AM–5 PM, Thursday 8 AM–6 PM and Friday 8 AM–12 PM.

**Q: Do you take insurance?**

Yes. We accept most major insurance plans. Call with your plan name and we'll confirm. Without insurance or with a high deductible, our Direct Primary Care membership may cost you less.

**Q: How much does Direct Primary Care cost?**

$99/month for an adult, $79/month for a spouse or partner, and $49/month per child ($276/month for a family of four). Membership includes unlimited visits, $0 copays, same- or next-day appointments and direct phone and text access to your provider.

**Q: Do you do DOT and CDL physicals?**

Yes. Owner Jenny Burds, DNP, ARNP is a certified medical examiner on the FMCSA National Registry. We also offer pre-employment physicals, 12-panel drug screens and work injury care. See occupational health.

**Q: Who are the providers?**

Three doctorate-prepared nurse practitioners: Jenny Burds, DNP, ARNP (owner, family medicine), Channah Chase, DNP, FNP-BC (family medicine) and Jenna Hefel, DNP, PMHNP-BC (psychiatric care for ages 12+). Meet the team.

**Q: Do you offer mental health care?**

Yes. We screen for anxiety and depression in primary care, and Jenna Hefel, DNP, PMHNP-BC provides psychiatric evaluations and medication management for patients 12 and older, including perinatal mental health.

Rooted in Peosta

### A clinic built by and for this community

The Burds family was among Peosta's founding families. Jenny Burds, DNP, opened the clinic in 2023 to give her hometown unhurried, relationship-first primary care close to home.

Local builders shaped our space, local artists' work hangs on our clinic walls, and we stay active in the community. We are proud to serve as a Platinum Sponsor of the 'Be A Light' 5K Mental Health Awareness Fun Run and champion fellow small businesses across Peosta and Dubuque.

New Patients

## Welcome. Getting started is simple.

We're accepting new patients of every age, from newborns to seniors. Here's everything you need to know before your first visit, with no surprises and no runaround.

What to bring

Three steps

### From first call to first visit

# Insurance vs. Direct Primary Care vs. Concierge | Burds Family Practice

URL: https://www.burdsfamilypractice.com/learn/dpc-vs-insurance-vs-concierge.html

← Back to Learning Hub & Resources

Understanding Your Options

## Insurance-Based, Direct Primary Care, or Concierge Medicine — Which One Is Actually Right for You?

The main difference between these three models comes down to who's in the room
between you and your doctor — and how you pay. Traditional insurance-based care routes everything
through a third party, creating prior authorizations, copays, and rushed appointments.
Concierge medicine adds a premium membership on top of insurance. Direct primary care
removes insurance from primary care entirely — you pay your provider directly, every month,
for unlimited access. Burds Family Practice offers both insurance-based and DPC
— and for most of our patients, DPC is the smarter, simpler choice.

The Three Models

### How Each One Works

Three very different approaches to primary care — same goal, very different experience.

Traditional

Insurance-Based Primary Care

The standard model — billing routed through your insurance company for every visit and service.

How you pay

Copays + deductibles + coinsurance

Unpredictable out-of-pocket costs

Typical patient panel

1,500 – 2,500 patients per provider

Less time per patient

Appointment wait

Days to weeks for non-urgent visits

Visit length

10–15 minutes typical

Direct provider access

Through office staff and portal

Available at Burds

✓ Yes

✦ Our Recommendation

Direct Primary Care

A flat monthly membership. No insurance billing. Unlimited primary care access — and a provider who actually knows you.

How you pay

Flat monthly membership fee

No copays, no deductibles, no surprise bills

Typical patient panel

300 – 600 patients per provider

More time, better continuity

Appointment wait

Same-day or next-day

Visit length

As long as you need

Direct provider access

Phone, text, and telehealth — directly

Available at Burds

✓ Yes — from $99/month

Premium

Concierge Medicine

Premium annual membership plus ongoing insurance billing. Enhanced access at a significantly higher cost.

How you pay

Annual membership + insurance billing

Membership fees on top of copays and deductibles

Typical patient panel

400 – 600 patients per provider

Appointment wait

Same or next day

Visit length

Longer than traditional

Direct provider access

Phone and direct messaging

Available at Burds

No — we don't offer this model

What It Actually Costs

### The Hidden Cost of "Free" Insurance-Based Care

Most people think of insurance-based primary care as low-cost because the copay
is all they see at the time of the visit. But that copay is only one piece of what
you're actually paying.

Every pay period, a health insurance premium is deducted from your paycheck —
whether you've used your insurance that month or not. According to the 2025 KFF
Employer Health Benefits Survey, the average employee contributes $571 per month
out of their own paycheck toward a family health insurance premium. That's
$6,850 a year — gone before you've seen a single doctor.

Then add the per-visit costs. Copays of $25 to $60 each time you come in. A deductible
— often $1,500 to $6,000 or more for a family — that has to be met before your insurance
pays much of anything. Surprise bills from coding errors or denied claims. The cost of
not going in when you should have because you didn't want to trigger another charge.

When you add it all up — premium, copays, deductibles, and out-of-pocket expenses —
traditional insurance-based primary care is far from free. And unlike your DPC membership,
not a single dollar of that premium is predictable, transparent, or in your control.

Insurance-Based

Premium + copays + deductible + surprises

Money leaves your paycheck every two weeks regardless of use. Then you pay again at every visit. Then again if you hit your deductible. The total is different every year — and almost impossible to predict.

Direct Primary Care at Burds ✦

One flat monthly fee. That's it.

$99/month for a single adult. $276/month for a family of four. No copays. No deductibles on primary care. No surprise bills. Ever. You know exactly what you're paying — every month, every year.

Concierge Medicine

Premium + membership + copays. All three.

Concierge medicine layers a premium membership fee — often $2,000 to $10,000 per year — on top of your existing insurance premium and copays. You pay more at every level.

DPC doesn't replace your health insurance — it replaces the part that was costing you the most.

You'll still want insurance for hospitalizations, specialist care, imaging, and emergencies.
But because your DPC membership covers the visits you use most — sick visits, annual physicals,
chronic condition management, telehealth — many of our members are able to switch to a
lower-cost, higher-deductible health plan and come out ahead overall.

Burds Family Practice DPC

no prior authorizations, no explanation of benefits to decode.

Direct Primary Care at Burds

Is DPC Right for You?

### Who Does Best with Direct Primary Care

DPC isn't for everyone — but for many of our patients, it's a significantly better experience at a comparable or lower total cost.

DPC tends to be the right fit for…

##### Patients who value access, clarity, and relationship

- Self-employed individuals and freelancers who pay their own healthcare costs

- Small business owners and their employees

- Families with children who need frequent sick visits

- Patients managing one or more chronic conditions

- Anyone on a high-deductible health plan tired of paying out of pocket for every visit

- Patients who've felt rushed, overlooked, or underserved in the traditional system

- Anyone who wants to text their provider directly instead of playing phone tag

- Families who want predictable, budgetable healthcare costs

Insurance-based may still make sense if…

##### The traditional model fits your situation

- Your employer covers most of your insurance premium and copays

- You rarely need primary care and have low out-of-pocket costs currently

- You have a complex medical history requiring frequent specialist coordination billed through insurance

- You prefer not to pay a monthly fee for healthcare regardless of usage

Burds Family Practice accepts both insurance and DPC members.
We'll never pressure you — but we're happy to walk through the numbers
to help you decide what makes sense for your family.

Common Questions

### Frequently Asked Questions

What is direct primary care (DPC)?

Direct primary care is a membership-based healthcare model where patients pay a flat monthly fee directly to their provider — with no insurance billing, no copays, and no surprise charges. The membership covers unlimited visits, same-day or next-day appointments, telehealth, chronic condition management, and direct access to your provider by phone or text. At Burds Family Practice in Peosta, Iowa, DPC membership starts at $99 per month for a single adult, $79 per month for a spouse, and $49 per month per child.

What is the difference between direct primary care and concierge medicine?

Direct primary care and concierge medicine are both membership-based models, but they differ significantly in cost and insurance involvement. DPC replaces insurance billing for primary care entirely — patients pay a monthly fee and the practice covers primary care with no copays or deductibles. Concierge medicine charges a premium annual membership fee — typically $2,000 to $10,000 per year — and still bills insurance on top of that fee. DPC is designed to be affordable and accessible to middle-income families. Concierge medicine is positioned as a premium, luxury service.

Do I still need health insurance if I join a DPC practice?

Yes. Direct primary care covers primary care services — your everyday healthcare needs, chronic condition management, preventive care, and sick visits. It does not replace insurance for hospitalizations, specialist referrals, imaging, surgery, or emergencies. Most DPC patients pair their membership with a lower-cost, higher-deductible health plan or a health sharing plan, since DPC handles the high-frequency, lower-cost visits that would otherwise eat through a deductible quickly.

How much does direct primary care cost at Burds Family Practice?

Burds Family Practice DPC membership is $99 per month for a single adult, $79 per month for a spouse or partner, and $49 per month per child. A family of four would pay $276 per month — with unlimited primary care visits, same-day appointments, telehealth access, and no copays or deductibles for covered primary care services.

Who is direct primary care right for?

Direct primary care is a strong fit for self-employed individuals and small business owners, families looking for predictable monthly costs, patients with high-deductible health plans who want to reduce out-of-pocket spending on primary care, anyone who wants same-day access and longer appointments, and patients who are frustrated with rushed visits and insurance complexity in the traditional model. Burds Family Practice in Peosta, Iowa offers DPC for patients of all ages.

Does Burds Family Practice accept insurance?

Yes. Burds Family Practice in Peosta, Iowa accepts both insurance-based patients and DPC members. We offer both models because we know different patients have different needs and situations. Our team is happy to walk through the comparison with you to help you decide which model makes sense for your family.

### Ready to try primary care the way it should be?

Join as a DPC member and get same-day access, a provider who knows you, and no surprise bills — ever. Starting at $99/month.
Join as a DPC Member
Call Us: (563) 588-6659

# Independent Practice vs. Large Health Systems | Burds Family Practice

URL: https://www.burdsfamilypractice.com/learn/independent-vs-health-system.html

← Back to Learning Hub & Resources

Understanding Your Options

## Independent Practice vs. Large Health Systems — Who's Actually Making Decisions About Your Care?

The main difference between an independent practice and a hospital-owned or
corporate health system comes down to one question: who does your provider
answer to? In an independent practice, the provider answers to you — the patient.
Clinical decisions are made based on your individual needs. In a hospital-owned or
corporate system, providers answer to administrators, efficiency targets, and
system-wide protocols. The care may still be good. But it is structurally different —
and research shows patients feel that difference.
Burds Family Practice is independently owned — and that's a
deliberate choice.

Side by Side

### What Each Model Looks Like in Practice

✦ Burds Family Practice

Independent Practice

Who makes clinical decisions
Your provider — based on your history, your goals, and your needs. No external protocol required.

Who owns the practice
A healthcare provider. At Burds, an ARNP/FNP who built this practice from the ground up and lives in this community.

Time with your provider
As long as your visit requires. The schedule is built around patients, not productivity metrics.

Provider continuity
You see the same provider. They know your name, your family, your history, and your preferences.

Community accountability
Your provider is your neighbor. The success of this practice depends entirely on the trust of this community.

Billing and costs
Transparent pricing with no surprise charges. No facility fees added to your bill.

Provider burnout
Independent providers report significantly lower burnout — which directly affects the quality and consistency of your care.

VS

Hospital / Corporate System

Large Health System

Who makes clinical decisions
Your provider — but within system-wide protocols, prior authorization requirements, and productivity expectations set by administrators.

Who owns the practice
A hospital system, insurance company, or private equity firm. Ownership priorities are financial and organizational, not clinical.

Time with your provider
Structured around efficiency. Studies show hospital-employed providers average 13.3 minutes per visit — compared to 18.5 in independent practices.

Provider continuity
High turnover in employed settings. You may see a different provider at each visit, or your provider may leave the system entirely.

Community accountability
Decisions are made at the system level — often by administrators in another city — not by someone invested in your specific community.

Billing and costs
Hospital-owned practices often add facility fees to standard office visits — charges that don't appear in independent practices. Patients are frequently surprised.

Provider burnout
100% of health system-based providers surveyed reported some level of burnout, vs. 15% of independent providers who reported none at all.

The trend toward consolidation is beginning to reverse as providers seek autonomy and patient-centered practice

What's Been Happening

### The Consolidation Problem — and Why It Matters to You

Over the past decade, independent medical practices have been disappearing at a significant rate.
In 2012, nearly half of all physicians owned or worked in an independent practice.
By 2022, that number had fallen to 30%. By early 2024, over 77% of physicians
were employed by a hospital, health system, or corporate entity.

This shift wasn't driven by patient preference — it was driven by financial pressure,
administrative burden, and aggressive acquisition by hospital systems and private equity firms.
And it has had real, measurable effects on patient experience.

What typically happens when an independent practice is acquired

At acquisition

Practice branding and signage changes. Administrative staff are replaced or reduced. Billing is consolidated into the system.

Within 6–12 months

Facility fees appear on your bill. Hospital-owned practices can charge a facility fee on top of the standard office visit charge — a fee that didn't exist before acquisition and that most patients don't notice until they open their explanation of benefits.

Appointment access

Patient panels increase as the system optimizes for volume. Wait times grow. Visit durations shorten. Your provider is seeing more patients in the same amount of time.

Clinical decisions

Prior authorization requirements increase. System-wide formularies restrict prescription options. Referral decisions are influenced by which specialists are in the system's network.

Provider turnover

Physicians employed by hospital systems report significantly higher burnout. Many leave — and the provider you chose is replaced by someone who doesn't know you.

Why This Matters Here

### In Eastern Iowa, Independent Practice Means Something

🌾

#### Small-town healthcare deserves small-town accountability.

In rural and small-town communities, the stakes of consolidation are higher.
When a large health system acquires the only primary care practice in a community,
patients have nowhere else to go — and the system knows it.
At Burds Family Practice, we are independently owned because we believe your
provider should be accountable to you — not to a board of directors in another city.
We built this practice in Peosta because this is our community.
The mission of bringing quality healthcare to the community we call home isn't a tagline.
It's why we structured our practice the way we did.

Healthcare consolidation has been particularly aggressive in Iowa and the Midwest.
As hospital systems expand their footprint in smaller markets, independent practices
become increasingly rare — and increasingly valuable. Choosing an independent practice
isn't just a personal preference. It's a vote for the kind of healthcare your
community keeps access to.

Common Questions

### Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between an independent medical practice and a hospital-owned practice?

An independent medical practice is owned and operated by a healthcare provider — not a hospital system, insurance company, or private equity firm. The provider makes clinical and operational decisions based on patient needs. A hospital-owned or corporate practice operates under the priorities of a larger organization, where standardized protocols, productivity metrics, and system-wide financial goals influence how care is delivered. Research shows patients of independent physicians report 26% higher satisfaction rates and spend significantly more time with their provider per visit.

Do patients get better care at independent practices?

Research consistently shows that patients at independent practices report higher satisfaction, stronger provider relationships, and more time with their doctor. A 2023 study found that physicians in independent practices spend an average of 18.5 minutes per patient visit compared to 13.3 minutes in hospital-owned practices. Among patients who prefer independent practices, 78% cite a stronger doctor-patient relationship, 60% report greater trust, and 57% say the quality of care is higher.

Why are so many doctor's offices now owned by hospitals or corporations?

The percentage of physicians in independent practice declined from 48.5% in 2012 to 30.1% by 2022, driven largely by financial pressure, administrative burden, and the rising cost of running a practice. Hospital systems and private equity firms have aggressively acquired independent practices over the past decade. As of January 2024, 77.6% of physicians were employed by hospitals, health systems, or corporate entities. However, the trend has begun to slow as more physicians seek to return to independent or physician-led settings.

Is Burds Family Practice an independent practice?

Yes. Burds Family Practice in Peosta, Iowa is independently owned and operated — not affiliated with a hospital system, insurance company, or corporate entity. Clinical decisions are made by the provider based on patient needs, not system-wide protocols or productivity metrics.

What happens to patient care when a practice is acquired by a hospital system?

When an independent practice is acquired by a hospital system or corporate entity, patients typically experience longer wait times, shorter appointment durations, and facility fees added to billing that didn't exist before. Clinical decisions may increasingly reflect system-wide protocols rather than individual patient needs. Provider turnover often increases as physicians in hospital-employed settings report significantly higher burnout rates.

### Healthcare that answers to you — not a system.

Burds Family Practice is independently owned, community-rooted, and built around your needs. Accepting new patients.

# Mental Health: Primary Care vs. Specialist | Burds Family Practice

URL: https://www.burdsfamilypractice.com/learn/mental-health-primarycare-vs-specialist.html

← Back to Learning Hub & Resources

Patient Guide

## Mental Health at Your Primary Care Provider vs. a Specialist — Who Should You See?

The short answer: start with primary care. For mild to moderate anxiety,
depression, ADHD, and stable mental health conditions, your primary care provider can
diagnose, treat, and prescribe — often faster and more affordably than a specialist.
When your needs are more complex, more severe, or not responding to initial treatment,
that's when psychiatry steps in. At Burds, we're honest about where that line is —
and we have strong referral relationships for when you need them.

Know Your Options

### Three Types of Mental Health Providers — What Each One Does

Mental health care can involve several different provider types. Understanding who does what helps you get to the right person faster.

Your First Stop

Primary Care Provider

Diagnoses, prescribes, manages, and coordinates your overall mental health care as part of whole-person medicine.

Can prescribe?

Yes — antidepressants, anti-anxiety, ADHD medications

Best for

Mild to moderate anxiety, depression, ADHD, stable mental health conditions

Wait times

Typically shorter — same or next week

Whole-person care

Yes — mental health connected to physical health in one record

At Burds

We treat mild to moderate conditions and refer when appropriate

When You Need More

Psychiatrist

A physician specializing in mental health — advanced training, broader medication range, and expertise in complex or severe conditions.

Can prescribe?

Yes — full range including controlled substances and advanced medications

Best for

Moderate to severe conditions, complex diagnoses, treatment-resistant cases, bipolar disorder, PTSD, psychosis

Wait times

Often weeks to months — high demand in most markets

Whole-person care

Focused on psychiatric conditions — coordinates with your PCP

At Burds

We refer here when your needs exceed primary care — with warm handoffs to local resources

Talk Therapy

Therapist / Counselor

Provides counseling, psychotherapy, and behavioral health support — does not prescribe medication.

Can prescribe?

No — therapy only, no medication management

Best for

Processing, coping skills, trauma, relationship issues, ongoing behavioral health support — often alongside medication

Wait times

Varies widely — can be significant in rural markets

Works with

Often paired with primary care or psychiatry for comprehensive care

At Burds

We refer to and coordinate with local therapists and counselors as part of your care plan

Our Scope at Burds

### What We Treat — and When We Refer

We're honest about what primary care does well in mental health and where
a specialist is the better call. Here's exactly where we draw the line.

We Handle This at Burds

##### Primary care mental health — our scope

- Mild to moderate anxiety — diagnosis, medication, and monitoring

- Mild to moderate depression — diagnosis, medication management, and follow-up

- ADHD — evaluation and medication management for established patients

- Stable, well-managed mental health conditions — ongoing medication and monitoring

- Screening for mental health concerns as part of routine care

- Initial evaluation when you're not sure what's going on

- Ruling out physical causes of mental health symptoms — thyroid, anemia, hormones

- Coordinating your care with therapists and specialists

We Refer to Psychiatry or Behavioral Health

##### When you need more than primary care

- Moderate to severe symptoms significantly affecting daily functioning

- Bipolar disorder — diagnosis, stabilization, and medication management

- PTSD — specialized evaluation and treatment protocols

- Schizophrenia or psychosis — requires psychiatric expertise

- Eating disorders — specialized evaluation and treatment

- Treatment-resistant depression — not responding after two or more medications

- Complex medication needs beyond primary care scope

- Situations requiring more intensive or specialized evaluation

We have strong referral relationships with psychiatry and behavioral health
providers nearby. When we refer, we do it with a warm handoff —
not just a name on a piece of paper.

Why Primary Care First

### The Whole-Person Advantage

One of the most underappreciated aspects of managing mental health in primary care
is that your mental health doesn't exist in isolation from the rest of your body.
And your primary care provider is the one who can see the whole picture.

🔗

##### Mental health and physical health are connected — your provider should be too

Fatigue that looks like depression could be a thyroid problem. Anxiety that isn't
responding to medication might be connected to blood sugar or hormone levels.
Sleep disruption worsens almost every mental health condition. Chronic pain and
mental health co-occur at significant rates. When your mental health care happens
in the same place as your physical care — with the same provider who has your
full record — those connections get caught. When they're siloed, they often don't.

Starting with primary care also means faster access. Psychiatrists in most markets
have wait times measured in weeks to months. If you're struggling with depression or
anxiety today, coming to see us first means getting evaluated, getting a plan,
and — if medication is appropriate — getting started while the referral process happens
in parallel.

Our Referral Network

#### A referral from Burds isn't the end of the conversation.

When your mental health needs exceed what primary care is equipped to manage,
we don't hand you a list of names and wish you luck. We have strong, established
relationships with psychiatry and behavioral health providers in the area —
providers we trust and coordinate with regularly. We'll make sure you get
connected, and we'll stay involved in your overall care while you do.

Many patients do best with a combination of primary care and specialist support —
psychiatry managing complex medication needs while Burds stays connected to the
rest of your health. That coordination doesn't happen automatically; it happens
because we make it a priority.

Common Questions

### Frequently Asked Questions

Can a primary care provider treat mental health conditions?

Yes. Primary care providers can diagnose and treat a range of mental health conditions — particularly mild to moderate anxiety, depression, and ADHD. At Burds Family Practice, we manage stable mental health conditions and prescribe for mild to moderate anxiety, depression, and ADHD. When a condition is more complex, more severe, or not responding to initial treatment, we refer to psychiatry or a behavioral health specialist.

What mental health conditions does Burds Family Practice treat?

Burds Family Practice manages stable mental health disorders and prescribes for mild to moderate anxiety, depression, and ADHD. We coordinate closely with psychiatry and behavioral health specialists for patients who need a higher level of care, and we have strong referral relationships with providers in the area.

When should I see a psychiatrist instead of my primary care provider?

You should see a psychiatrist when your symptoms are moderate to severe and affecting daily functioning, when you have a complex condition such as bipolar disorder, PTSD, schizophrenia, or treatment-resistant depression, when medications prescribed in primary care have not been effective, or when you need specialized evaluation or a broader range of treatment options. Burds Family Practice will refer you to psychiatry or a behavioral health specialist when your needs exceed what primary care is equipped to manage — with a warm handoff to trusted local providers.

What is the difference between a psychiatrist, a therapist, and a primary care provider for mental health?

A primary care provider can diagnose and prescribe medication for common mental health conditions like mild to moderate anxiety, depression, and ADHD, and can manage stable conditions as part of whole-person care. A psychiatrist is a physician specializing in mental health with advanced training in complex conditions and a broader range of medication options. A therapist provides talk therapy and counseling but cannot prescribe medication. The three often work together, with primary care as the entry point and coordinator.

Should I start with my primary care provider or go straight to a psychiatrist?

For most people experiencing mental health symptoms for the first time, starting with a primary care provider is the right first step. Your provider can rule out physical causes, assess the severity, prescribe initial medication if appropriate, and refer you to psychiatry or therapy if needed. Starting with primary care is typically faster — psychiatrists often have wait times of weeks to months — and your provider can coordinate your overall care as you get connected with the right resources.

### Not sure where to start?

Start with us. We'll assess where you are, talk through your options honestly, and make sure you get connected to the right care — whether that's here or somewhere else.

# Occupational Health: In-House vs. Third-Party | Burds Family Practice

URL: https://www.burdsfamilypractice.com/learn/occupational-health-inhouse-vs-thirdparty.html

← Back to Learning Hub & Resources

Employer Guide

## In-House Occupational Health vs. Third-Party Clinics — Why Where Your Employees Go Matters

The main difference between in-house occupational health and a third-party clinic
is relationship and context. Both can perform a DOT physical or collect a drug screen.
But when occupational health is handled by a primary care practice that also knows
your employees as patients, the care is connected — to their health history, to your
workplace, and to a provider who is accountable to your community.
Burds Family Practice offers a full occupational health menu for
employers in eastern Iowa — with the continuity of a primary care relationship
built in.

Side by Side

### How the Two Models Compare

✦ Burds Family Practice

In-House Occupational Health

Who handles it
Your employees' primary care provider — someone who knows their health history, their medications, and their baseline.

Relationship with the employer
Direct. One point of contact. A provider who understands your workplace, your industry, and your workforce over time.

Continuity of care
Occupational health findings connect to the employee's broader medical record. A work injury doesn't exist in isolation from the rest of their health.

Community accountability
Your provider is your neighbor. They are invested in the health and productivity of this community's workforce — not processing volume for a national chain.

Communication
Direct access to the provider — not a call center. Questions get answered by the person who performed the exam.

Return-to-work coordination
Easier and faster when the occupational health provider and the primary care provider are the same practice. No referral loops, no lost records.

VS

Third-Party Clinic

Standalone Occupational Health

Who handles it
A provider at a standalone clinic or urgent care chain with no prior knowledge of the employee's health history or baseline.

Relationship with the employer
Transactional. Each visit starts fresh. No ongoing relationship with your company or understanding of your specific workplace.

Continuity of care
Occupational health records stay in a separate system. If the employee has a related medical history, the examining provider may never know.

Community accountability
Often a regional or national chain. Staff turnover is high. The provider who examined your employee last year may not be there this year.

Communication
Typically through a central scheduling or results line. Getting answers can mean navigating hold queues and unfamiliar staff.

Return-to-work coordination
Requires coordination between separate systems. Records must be transferred, timelines can slip, and employees fall through the gaps.

Our Occupational Health Menu

### What Burds Offers Eastern Iowa Employers

A full occupational health menu — available to employers throughout Peosta,
Dyersville, and the greater Dubuque area. No need to send your employees
to a standalone clinic across town.

DOT Physicals

Required for commercial motor vehicle drivers. Performed by a certified medical examiner.

Pre-Employment Physicals

Baseline health assessments before an employee starts work — tailored to job requirements.

Drug Testing / Urine Screens

Pre-employment, random, post-accident, and reasonable suspicion drug screening.

Breath Alcohol Testing

DOT and non-DOT breath alcohol testing for employers with drug and alcohol policies.

Workers' Compensation Injury Care

Prompt evaluation and treatment of work-related injuries — with documentation for claims.

OSHA Compliance Exams

Medical surveillance and compliance exams required by OSHA standards for specific industries.

Return-to-Work Evaluations

Fitness-for-duty assessments to safely clear employees to return after injury or illness.

Immunizations & Flu Clinics

Workplace flu clinics and occupationally relevant immunizations for your workforce.

#### One practice. Your entire workforce.

Burds Family Practice serves employers across eastern Iowa — from single-owner businesses
to multi-employee operations. We set up employer accounts, communicate directly with HR
and safety managers, and provide the documentation your team needs without the runaround
of a high-volume chain clinic. Call us to discuss setting up an employer relationship.

Why Continuity Matters

### The Problem with Treating Occupational Health in Isolation

When an employee gets a DOT physical at a standalone clinic and sees their primary care
provider somewhere else entirely, those two providers are operating with incomplete
pictures of the same person's health. That gap has real consequences.

Third-Party Approach

##### The provider doing the exam doesn't know the employee

A DOT physical performed without knowledge of the employee's medical history, current medications, or chronic conditions relies entirely on what the employee self-reports in that moment. Conditions that should be flagged may not be — and conditions that are flagged may lack the context to be properly evaluated.

Burds Family Practice

##### Occupational health and primary care in the same record

When your employee is also a Burds patient, their occupational health visits connect to a complete clinical picture. A DOT physical performed by a provider who already knows the employee's blood pressure history, sleep patterns, and medication list is a meaningfully more thorough exam — for the employer and the employee.

In Practice

### What a Workers' Comp Injury Looks Like at Each

Here's how the same workplace injury plays out depending on where the employee goes for care.

Third-Party Clinic

1

Employee is injured. Employer directs them to the nearest standalone occupational health clinic or urgent care chain.

2

Employee is seen by a provider who has never met them. Health history is collected from scratch.

3

Treatment and documentation are completed. Records stay in the clinic's separate system.

4

Return-to-work requires coordination between the occupational clinic, the employee's primary care provider, and the employer — often across multiple calls and records requests.

5

Next time the employee needs occupational health, the process starts from scratch again — possibly with a different provider.

Burds Family Practice

1

Employee is injured. Employer calls Burds — the same practice that already handles their occupational health account.

2

Employee is seen same-day or next-day by a provider who already knows their health history, baseline vitals, and medications.

3

Treatment and documentation are completed in the same record as the employee's primary care history.

4

Return-to-work evaluation is handled by the same practice — no records transfer, no coordination gap, no delay.

5

Employer has a direct line to the provider. Questions are answered by the person who performed the exam.

### Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between in-house occupational health and a third-party occupational health clinic?

In-house occupational health means your employees receive work-related health services at a primary care practice that also knows them as patients. A third-party occupational health clinic handles those same services in a standalone setting with no connection to the employee's broader health history. The key difference is continuity — when occupational health and primary care are under one roof, the provider has full context, and the employer has a single point of contact for their workforce health needs.

What occupational health services does Burds Family Practice offer?

Burds Family Practice in Peosta, Iowa offers DOT physicals, pre-employment physicals, drug testing and urine screens, breath alcohol testing, workers' compensation injury care, OSHA compliance exams, return-to-work evaluations, and immunizations including flu clinics. Services are available to employers throughout the Peosta, Dyersville, and greater Dubuque area of eastern Iowa.

Does Burds Family Practice do DOT physicals?

Yes. Burds Family Practice in Peosta, Iowa performs DOT physicals for commercial motor vehicle drivers. DOT exams are required by federal law for drivers of commercial vehicles and must be performed by a certified medical examiner. Burds serves employers and drivers throughout eastern Iowa including the Dubuque, Peosta, and Dyersville areas.

Does Burds Family Practice offer employer drug testing?

Yes. Burds Family Practice offers pre-employment drug testing, urine screens, and breath alcohol testing for employers. These services are available to businesses in the Peosta, Dyersville, and greater Dubuque area of eastern Iowa.

Why should employers use a primary care practice for occupational health instead of a standalone clinic?

When occupational health is handled by a primary care practice, employers benefit from a provider who knows the workforce, communicates directly with the employer, and can identify health trends that affect productivity and safety. Employees benefit because their work-related care is connected to their overall health history. Third-party clinics handle the transactional services competently, but they have no ongoing relationship with the employee or the employer — every visit starts from zero.

# Preventive Care: What's Covered | Burds Family Practice

URL: https://www.burdsfamilypractice.com/learn/preventive-care-whats-covered.html

← Back to Learning Hub & Resources

Patient Guide

## Preventive Care — What's Covered, What Costs Money, and Why It Matters

Most people leave preventive care on the table.
Under the Affordable Care Act, your insurance is required to cover a broad range
of preventive services — screenings, immunizations, and wellness visits —
at absolutely no cost to you. No copay. No deductible. No coinsurance.
But there's a catch: you have to know what's covered, come in to get it,
and understand the difference between a preventive visit and a sick visit
so you don't end up with a surprise bill.
This guide explains all of it.

The Basics

### Preventive Visit vs. Sick Visit — They're Billed Differently

This is the distinction that causes more patient confusion — and more surprise bills —
than almost any other aspect of primary care billing. Understanding it before your
appointment can save you money.

Preventive Visit — Typically $0 Cost

##### You come in to stay well

- Annual wellness exam or physical — no symptoms, no specific concern

- Routine screenings appropriate for your age and sex

- Immunizations and vaccines

- Health risk assessment and counseling

- Covered at no cost under the ACA for most non-grandfathered plans

- Must be with an in-network provider to be covered at $0

- Must be the primary reason for the visit — not combined with a sick concern

Sick Visit — Subject to Copay / Deductible

##### You come in because something is wrong

- You have a specific symptom or concern — cold, ear pain, rash, chest tightness

- Follow-up for a chronic condition — blood pressure check, diabetes management

- Evaluation of a new or existing problem

- Prescription refill tied to an ongoing condition

- Billed as a diagnostic or office visit — subject to your copay and deductible

- Even if you come in for your annual and raise a new concern, that concern may be billed separately as a sick visit

##### Why your annual physical sometimes results in a bill

This is one of the most common and frustrating billing surprises in primary care.
You schedule your annual physical — it's supposed to be free. But you mention
your knee has been bothering you, or you bring up a new medication concern,
and suddenly you get a bill.

Here's why: insurance distinguishes between preventive care and problem-focused
care. The moment your provider addresses a specific clinical concern beyond the
preventive screening, that additional service may be billed separately — and
that portion is subject to your copay or deductible.

The fix: if you have specific concerns beyond your annual wellness exam,
let us know upfront. We may recommend scheduling a separate visit so the preventive
portion stays covered at $0 and you know exactly what to expect for the rest.

What the Law Says

### What the ACA Requires Your Insurance to Cover

The Affordable Care Act requires most private health insurance plans to cover
a broad list of preventive services at no cost to you — as long as you see
an in-network provider and the preventive service is the primary reason for your visit.

⚖️

##### Confirmed in 2025: These coverage requirements are still the law

In June 2025, the United States Supreme Court upheld the constitutionality
of the ACA's preventive services mandate, confirming that insurers remain
required by federal law to cover USPSTF-recommended preventive services
without cost sharing. Your no-cost preventive care coverage is intact.

The services covered fall into four categories: recommendations from the
U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF), immunization recommendations from
the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), children's preventive
services under the Bright Futures guidelines, and women's preventive services
under HRSA guidelines.

Note: grandfathered health plans — plans that have been in continuous existence
since before March 23, 2010 — may not be required to cover all preventive services.
Short-term health plans are also exempt. If you're unsure whether your plan qualifies,
call your insurance company and ask.

What's Included

### Common Preventive Services Covered at No Cost

This is not an exhaustive list — the full set of covered services depends on your
age, sex, health history, and specific plan. But these are the services most
adults and families should expect to access at no cost.

Adults of all ages — once per year

Why This Matters

### Preventive Care Isn't Just Paperwork — It Saves Lives

The reason insurance is required to cover these services isn't bureaucratic.
It's because catching things early — before symptoms appear — consistently
leads to better outcomes, less invasive treatment, and lower long-term costs.

#### The best time to find a problem is before you have symptoms.

Colon cancer caught at stage 1 has a 90%+ survival rate. Caught at stage 4, that drops
dramatically. High blood pressure identified and treated early prevents heart attacks
and strokes. Diabetes caught in the prediabetes stage is often reversible with lifestyle
changes alone. Depression screened and identified early responds better to treatment.
Preventive care isn't a formality — it's the most efficient investment you can make
in your own health.

At Burds Family Practice, your annual wellness visit is how we stay ahead of things
for you. We track your numbers over time, flag changes, order the screenings you're
due for, and make sure you're not leaving free, potentially life-saving care on the table.

If you haven't had a wellness exam in the past year — or you've been skipping them
because you assumed there would be a charge — call us. For most patients with
non-grandfathered insurance, the visit is covered at no cost.

Common Questions

### Frequently Asked Questions

What is preventive care?

Preventive care refers to health services designed to prevent illness, detect conditions early, or manage risk factors before they become serious problems. It includes annual wellness visits, screenings, immunizations, and counseling. Unlike a sick visit — where you come in because something is wrong — preventive care is proactive. You come in to stay well and catch things before they develop into bigger problems.

Is preventive care covered by insurance?

Under the Affordable Care Act, most private health insurance plans are required to cover a broad range of preventive services at no cost to the patient — no copay, no deductible, no coinsurance. This applies when the service is performed by an in-network provider and is the primary reason for the visit. In June 2025, the Supreme Court upheld the constitutionality of these requirements, confirming that insurers must continue to cover USPSTF-recommended preventive services.

What is the difference between a preventive visit and a sick visit?

A preventive visit — also called a wellness exam or annual physical — is scheduled when you are not sick and focuses on screenings, immunizations, and health risk assessment. It is typically covered at no cost by insurance. A sick visit is scheduled because you have a specific symptom or concern, and is billed differently — usually subject to a copay or deductible. If you come in for your annual physical and also bring up a new health concern at the same visit, your insurance may bill that second issue separately as a sick visit charge.

Why does my annual physical sometimes result in a bill?

If you come in for a preventive visit and your provider addresses a new or separate clinical concern during the same appointment, that additional service may be billed separately and subject to your copay or deductible. Insurance distinguishes between preventive care and problem-focused care. To avoid surprise bills, let your provider know upfront if you want to keep the visit purely preventive, or schedule a separate appointment for any additional concerns.

What preventive services are covered at no cost?

Preventive services covered at no cost under the ACA include annual wellness visits, blood pressure screening, cholesterol screening, diabetes screening, colorectal cancer screening, mammograms, cervical cancer screening, depression screening, obesity counseling, lung cancer screening for high-risk adults, immunizations including flu shots and COVID-19 vaccines, and many more. The specific services covered depend on your age, sex, health history, and insurance plan.

### When did you last have a wellness visit?

If it's been more than a year — or you've never scheduled one — call us. For most patients, it's covered at no cost. It takes an hour and it matters.

# Telehealth vs. In-Person Visits | Burds Family Practice

URL: https://www.burdsfamilypractice.com/learn/telehealth-vs-inperson.html

← Back to Learning Hub & Resources

Patient Guide

## Telehealth vs. In-Person — Our Honest Take

At Burds Family Practice, we are an in-person practice first.
Telehealth has its place — for weight loss follow-ups and certain mental health
medication check-ins for established patients — but the vast majority of what
we do requires being in the room together. Primary care is a hands-on discipline.
We'd rather see you properly than risk missing something because a video call
was more convenient.

The Honest Comparison

### What Telehealth Can and Can't Do

Telehealth is a useful tool for the right situations. The problem is that it gets
used for too many situations where an in-person exam would catch things a video
call simply cannot. Here's how we think about it.

Limited Use at Burds

Telehealth

What it allows
Conversation and visual observation. Your provider can see you, hear your symptoms, and review your record.

What it cannot do
Listen to your heart and lungs. Palpate your abdomen. Look in your ears. Feel a lump. Run a rapid test. Perform any procedure. These things require being in the room.

Where it works
When the provider already has a complete clinical picture and the visit is purely about monitoring something stable — not evaluating something new.

Where it falls short
Anywhere a physical finding could change the clinical picture. Research shows 6.2% of telehealth visits require an in-person follow-up within 7 days — because something was missed remotely.

At Burds
Used only for weight loss follow-ups and select mental health medication check-ins for established patients with a stable, well-documented condition.

VS

✦ Our Standard

In-Person Visit

What it allows
A full clinical assessment — physical exam, point-of-care testing, lab draws, procedures, and the kind of observation that only happens when you're in the same room.

What it adds
Things your provider can hear, feel, see up close, and measure in real time. Often it's a physical finding — not what you say — that changes the diagnosis.

Where it excels
Everywhere. There is no clinical situation where an in-person exam provides less information than a telehealth visit.

The tradeoff
Requires travel. We know that. But we offer same-day appointments and try to make getting here as easy as possible — because getting it right matters more than getting it fast.

At Burds
Our default for essentially all care. Sick visits, physicals, chronic condition management, mental health, new concerns, follow-ups — we want to see you in person.

Our Telehealth Policy

### Where We Use Telehealth — and Where We Don't

We offer telehealth for a small number of visit types where it genuinely serves the patient —
not as a default convenience option. Here's exactly where we draw the line.

Telehealth — Available at Burds

##### Where virtual visits make sense for us

- Weight loss medication follow-ups — monitoring progress and adjusting dosing for established patients

- Mental health medication check-ins — for stable, established patients whose condition is well-documented and not in flux

In both of these cases, the provider already has a complete clinical picture,
no physical exam findings are expected to change the plan, and the visit
is purely about monitoring and adjusting something already in motion.

In-Person — Our Standard for Everything Else

##### Where we want to see you in the office

- Sick visits — colds, flu, infections, any acute illness

- Annual physicals and wellness exams

- New symptoms or concerns being evaluated for the first time

- Ear infections, sore throats, sinus concerns

- Chronic condition management — diabetes, blood pressure, thyroid

- Any concern requiring lab work, testing, or procedures

- Injuries or wounds

- New mental health concerns

- Anything where a physical finding could matter

Our Philosophy

### Why We Default to In-Person Care

The telehealth boom that came out of the pandemic was born from necessity — and it
demonstrated that some visit types genuinely work well virtually. But it also
normalized a convenience-first approach to care that we think has gone too far.

Primary care is a physical discipline. The stethoscope, the otoscope, the hands
on your abdomen — these aren't formalities. They're the exam. And the exam is
where findings get made that change what happens next.

#### We'd rather see you and get it right than guess from a screen.

If you come in with an ear that hurts and we look inside and see a normal ear drum,
we know you don't have an ear infection and we look for something else. If we do that
visit by video, we prescribe based on what you're telling us — which may or may not
match what we'd actually find. That gap matters. We're not willing to trade clinical
accuracy for convenience.

6.2%

##### of telehealth visits require an in-person follow-up within 7 days

Compared to 1.3% of in-person visits. That gap exists because some conditions
cannot be fully assessed without physical examination — and when they're managed
remotely, patients often end up needing to come in anyway. We'd rather skip
the extra step and just see you.

What In-Person Makes Possible

### Things That Require Being in the Room

This is the list that matters most when you're deciding whether a telehealth visit
is appropriate. If any of these are potentially relevant to your concern,
you need to come in.

Auscultation — listening to heart and lung sounds

Otoscope exam — looking inside the ear canal

Abdominal palpation — feeling for tenderness, masses, or organ changes

Rapid testing — strep, flu, COVID, urinalysis

Blood pressure, pulse, and oxygen measurement

Lab draws — blood work, cultures

Skin examination up close — rashes, lesions, wounds

Lymph node assessment — palpating for swelling

Throat and tonsil examination

Wound care, suturing, and procedures

Injections and immunizations

EKG and other diagnostic testing

Common Questions

### Frequently Asked Questions

Does Burds Family Practice offer telehealth visits?

Burds Family Practice offers telehealth for a limited and deliberate set of visit types — primarily weight loss medication follow-ups and certain mental health medication check-ins for established patients with stable, well-documented conditions. The vast majority of care at Burds is delivered in person. We believe most clinical concerns are better served by a hands-on exam, and we'd rather see you than guess.

Why does Burds Family Practice prefer in-person visits?

Primary care is a hands-on discipline. Listening to heart and lungs, palpating an abdomen, examining a rash up close, looking in an ear — these things cannot be done over a video call. A telehealth visit can miss findings that an in-person exam would catch. Research shows that 6.2% of telehealth visits require a follow-up in-person appointment within 7 days. At Burds, we'd rather see you properly than risk missing something important because it was more convenient to do it virtually.

When is telehealth appropriate at Burds Family Practice?

At Burds, telehealth is used for weight loss follow-up appointments and select mental health medication check-ins for established patients whose condition is stable and well-documented. These are situations where the provider already has a complete clinical picture and the visit is about monitoring and adjusting — not evaluating something new.

Can I do a sick visit by telehealth at Burds?

No. Sick visits at Burds Family Practice are in-person. When you're ill, your provider needs to examine you — listen to your lungs, look in your ears and throat, assess your lymph nodes, and potentially run rapid tests. None of those things are possible over video. We offer same-day appointments for sick patients, so getting in quickly is rarely a barrier.

# Urgent Care vs. Primary Care vs. the ER | Burds Family Practice

Patient Guide

## Urgent Care vs. Primary Care vs. ER — Where Should You Actually Go?

The short answer: go to the ER for anything life-threatening.
Go to urgent care when your primary care provider isn't available and you can't wait.
Go to your primary care provider for everything else — it's less expensive, your provider
knows your history, and the care continues beyond a single visit.
If you're a Burds Family Practice DPC member, call or text us first.
Same-day access means you rarely need urgent care at all.

🚨

If you think it might be an emergency — go to the ER or call 911.
This guide is for non-emergency situations. When in doubt about whether something is serious, always err on the side of emergency care. No guide replaces clinical judgment in the moment.

The Three Options

### What Each Level of Care Is Designed For

These aren't interchangeable options — each setting is built for a different level of urgency, equipped differently, and priced very differently.

Common Questions

### Frequently Asked Questions

Should I go to urgent care or my primary care doctor?

If your primary care provider offers same-day appointments, go there first. Primary care is less expensive, your provider knows your history, and you'll receive continuity of care rather than a one-time visit. Urgent care is appropriate when your primary care provider is unavailable and you have a non-life-threatening condition that can't wait. At Burds Family Practice, DPC members have same-day access, which eliminates most reasons to visit urgent care.

When should I go to the emergency room?

Go to the emergency room — or call 911 — for any condition that is life-threatening or rapidly worsening. This includes chest pain or pressure, difficulty breathing, signs of stroke (face drooping, arm weakness, speech difficulty), severe bleeding that won't stop, loss of consciousness, severe allergic reaction, major trauma or injury, and seizures. The ER is equipped with specialists, imaging, labs, and surgical capability around the clock. It is not the right setting for conditions that are uncomfortable but stable.

How much does an ER visit cost compared to urgent care or primary care?

Emergency room visits average $1,500 to $3,000 or more — even for conditions that are not life-threatening. Urgent care visits average $150 to $250 without insurance. Primary care visits average $75 to $150 with an insurance copay. For Burds Family Practice DPC members, primary care visits are $0 — covered by the flat monthly membership — making same-day primary care the most affordable option for non-emergency care.

Why do DPC members go to urgent care less often?

Most urgent care visits happen because patients can't reach their primary care provider quickly enough. With direct primary care at Burds Family Practice, members have same-day or next-day appointments, direct access to their provider by phone or text, and telehealth for concerns that don't require an in-person visit. When you can reach your own provider immediately, the need for urgent care drops significantly — and so does the cost.

Can I call Burds Family Practice after hours?

DPC members at Burds Family Practice have direct access to their provider by phone or text — including after-hours for urgent concerns. This means you can often get guidance on whether a symptom requires urgent care or the ER, or handle the concern directly without leaving home. This is one of the most valued benefits of DPC membership.

# Viral vs. Bacterial Infection | Burds Family Practice

URL: https://www.burdsfamilypractice.com/learn/viral-vs-bacterial-infection.html

← Back to Learning Hub & Resources

Patient Education

## Viral vs. Bacterial Infection — What's the Difference and Why Does It Matter?

The main difference between a viral and bacterial infection is what's causing
it — and that determines how it's treated. Bacterial infections can be treated with antibiotics.
Viral infections cannot — antibiotics have no effect on viruses whatsoever.
Both can cause similar symptoms, which is why it's often difficult to tell them apart
without a clinical evaluation. When in doubt, call your provider before assuming
you need an antibiotic.

The Basics

### Two Very Different Types of Infection

Viruses and bacteria are fundamentally different organisms — and understanding that difference is the foundation of knowing why they're treated so differently.

Caused by a virus

Viral Infection

Viruses are microscopic particles that cannot reproduce on their own — they invade your cells and use them to replicate.

What causes it

A virus — such as rhinovirus, influenza, COVID-19, RSV, or norovirus

Treated with antibiotics?

No — antibiotics have zero effect on viruses

Antiviral medications exist for some specific viruses

Typical duration

7–10 days for most respiratory viruses

Symptoms often peak then gradually improve

How your body clears it

Your immune system fights the virus

Treatment focuses on managing symptoms while this happens

Onset pattern

Often gradual — symptoms build over 1–2 days

Contagious?

Yes — most viral infections spread person to person

Caused by bacteria

Bacterial Infection

Bacteria are single-celled microorganisms that can reproduce independently and cause tissue damage as they multiply.

What causes it

Bacteria — such as streptococcus, E. coli, or Staphylococcus

Treated with antibiotics?

Yes — antibiotics kill bacteria or stop their growth

The right antibiotic for the right bacteria matters

Typical duration

Clears in 7–14 days with the right antibiotic

Without treatment, bacterial infections can worsen

How it's cleared

Antibiotics — prescribed by your provider

Complete the full course even if you feel better early

Onset pattern

Can be sudden — especially strep or UTI

Or secondary: developing after an initial viral illness

Contagious?

Some are, some aren't — depends on the bacteria

The Most Important Thing to Know

### Antibiotics Only Work on Bacteria

This is the single most consequential distinction between viral and bacterial infections —
and it's one of the most misunderstood facts in everyday healthcare.

⚠️

##### Taking antibiotics for a viral infection doesn't help — and it can cause harm.

Antibiotics work by targeting specific structures or processes in bacterial cells.
Viruses don't have those structures. Giving a patient antibiotics for a cold, the flu,
or most sore throats and coughs does nothing to clear the virus — and contributes to
antibiotic resistance, one of the most serious public health threats
we face. Resistant bacteria are harder — and sometimes impossible — to treat.
This is why your provider won't prescribe antibiotics unless there's clinical reason
to believe a bacterial infection is present.

It's worth noting that most upper respiratory infections — colds, coughs, most sore throats,
most sinus congestion — are viral. The American Academy of Family Physicians notes that
antibiotics are frequently overprescribed for these illnesses, which is why your provider
will evaluate your symptoms carefully before prescribing.

Symptoms

### Why They're Hard to Tell Apart

Viral and bacterial infections share many of the same symptoms — which is exactly why
it can be difficult to know which one you have without clinical evaluation.
Here's how the symptom picture breaks down.

More common in viral

- Runny or stuffy nose

- Watery eyes

- Sneezing

- Diffuse muscle aches

- Gradual onset over 1–2 days

- Symptoms improve within 7–10 days

- Hoarse voice

- Cough without colored mucus

Can be either

- Fever

- Sore throat

- Fatigue

- Headache

- Cough

- Sinus congestion

- Ear pain

- Nausea

- Diarrhea

More common in bacterial

- Severe or sudden sore throat

- White patches on tonsils

- Thick, colored mucus (yellow/green)

- Localized pain (ear, sinus, throat)

- Symptoms persist beyond 10 days

- Symptoms worsen after initial improvement

- Burning or pain with urination (UTI)

- Skin redness, warmth, swelling

The most reliable clue: what happens over time

Viral infections typically follow a pattern of gradual onset, peak symptoms around days 2–4,
then gradual improvement. If your symptoms start improving then suddenly get worse —
or if they simply aren't improving after 7–10 days — that's a signal that a secondary
bacterial infection may have developed on top of the original viral illness. Call your provider.

Treatment

### How Each Is Treated

Viral Infection

##### Support your immune system while it does the work

- Rest — your body heals while you sleep

- Stay well hydrated — water, broth, electrolytes

- Over-the-counter symptom relief — ibuprofen or acetaminophen for fever and aches

- Decongestants or antihistamines for nasal symptoms

- Cough suppressants or expectorants as needed

- Honey and warm liquids for sore throat

- Antiviral medications for specific viruses — Tamiflu for flu, Paxlovid for COVID-19 — when prescribed by your provider

- Time — most resolve in 7–10 days

Bacterial Infection

##### Antibiotics — the right one, for the right duration

- Antibiotics prescribed by your provider

- Complete the full course — even if you feel better early

- The right antibiotic matters — your provider will match it to the likely bacteria

- A culture or rapid test may be needed to confirm the bacteria and guide treatment

- Symptom relief alongside antibiotics — rest, fluids, pain relievers

- Follow-up if symptoms don't improve within 48–72 hours of starting antibiotics

- Do not share antibiotics or use leftover antibiotics from a previous prescription

Common Illnesses

### Is It Viral or Bacterial? Common Examples

Here's how some of the most common illnesses break down — though your provider should always confirm, since some conditions can be caused by either.

Usually Viral

- Common cold (rhinovirus and others)

- Influenza (flu)

- COVID-19

- RSV

- Most coughs and bronchitis

- Stomach flu / norovirus

- Mononucleosis (mono)

- Chickenpox / shingles

- Most sore throats

- Most ear infections in adults

- Viral pink eye (conjunctivitis)

- Most sinus congestion within first 10 days

Usually Bacterial

- Strep throat

- Urinary tract infection (UTI)

- Most ear infections in children

- Bacterial sinus infection (after 10+ days)

- Bacterial pneumonia

- Lyme disease

- Whooping cough (pertussis)

- Cellulitis and skin infections

- Bacterial pink eye (conjunctivitis)

- H. pylori (stomach ulcers)

- Impetigo

- Bacterial meningitis
