When to Seek Care

### When to Call Your Provider

Many viral infections can be managed at home with rest and over-the-counter remedies.
But there are clear signals that you should reach out to your provider — whether
to rule out a bacterial infection, get antiviral treatment, or make sure something
more serious isn't developing.

#### Call Burds — don't wait it out — if you have:

- Symptoms lasting more than 7–10 days without improvement

- Symptoms that improve then suddenly worsen

- Fever above 103°F in an adult

- Any fever in an infant under 3 months

- Severe throat pain or difficulty swallowing

- Ear pain — especially in children

- Difficulty breathing or shortness of breath

- Burning or pain with urination

- Skin that is red, warm, swelling, or spreading

- You are immunocompromised or have chronic conditions

- You're just not sure — that's what we're here for

Burds Family Practice patients can call or text their provider directly with questions.
You don't have to guess whether you need to come in — just ask. That's one of the
most practical benefits of a primary care relationship.

Common Questions

### Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between a viral and bacterial infection?

Viral infections are caused by viruses — microscopic particles that require a living host to replicate and cannot survive independently. Bacterial infections are caused by bacteria — single-celled microorganisms that can reproduce on their own. The distinction matters because the treatments are fundamentally different: bacterial infections can be treated with antibiotics, while viral infections cannot. Antibiotics have no effect on viruses.

Can antibiotics treat a viral infection?

No. Antibiotics only work against bacteria — they have no effect on viruses. Taking antibiotics for a viral infection will not help you recover faster and contributes to antibiotic resistance, which is a serious public health problem. For viral infections, treatment focuses on managing symptoms while your immune system clears the virus. In some cases, antiviral medications are available for specific viruses such as influenza, herpes, and COVID-19.

How do I know if my infection is viral or bacterial?

Viral and bacterial infections often cause similar symptoms — fever, fatigue, sore throat, congestion — which makes it difficult to tell them apart without clinical evaluation. Viral infections often improve within 7 to 10 days, while bacterial infections may persist, worsen after initial improvement, or include localized pain such as severe throat pain, ear pain, or burning urination. The most reliable way to know is to see your provider, who can evaluate your symptoms and order a rapid test or culture if needed.

What are examples of viral infections?

Common viral infections include the common cold, influenza, COVID-19, RSV, most sore throats and coughs, mononucleosis, stomach flu caused by norovirus, chickenpox, and most cases of bronchitis. Most upper respiratory infections are viral — antibiotics are frequently overprescribed for these illnesses despite having no benefit.

What are examples of bacterial infections?

Common bacterial infections include strep throat, urinary tract infections, certain ear infections, bacterial pneumonia, Lyme disease, bacterial sinus infections that persist beyond 10 days, whooping cough, and skin infections like cellulitis and impetigo. These typically require antibiotic treatment prescribed by a provider.

When should I see a doctor for an infection?

See your provider if symptoms are severe, last more than 7 to 10 days, or worsen after an initial period of improvement. Also seek care for high fever above 103°F, severe throat pain, difficulty swallowing or breathing, ear pain, symptoms in a child under 3 months, or if you are immunocompromised. Your provider can determine whether your infection is viral or bacterial and whether treatment is needed. Burds Family Practice patients can call or text their provider directly for guidance.

### Not sure what you have? Just ask us.

Burds Family Practice patients can call or text their provider directly. You don't have to guess — we're here to help you figure it out.

# Baby Fever: When Is It Serious? Age-by-Age Guide

URL: https://www.burdsfamilypractice.com/blog/9ojrpkasesq9c2rcza21gbmrv5uq7b.html

← Resources & Blog
Community Health Blog

## My Baby Has a Fever — When Is It Serious?

Published Jul 6, 2026
2 min read
By Jennifer Burds, DNP, ARNP

Few things are more alarming for a new parent than a feverish baby. Your instinct is to do something — but it can be hard to know what. Here's what we tell families at Burds Family Practice every day.

### First: What Is Actually a Fever?

A fever is a rectal temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher. Ear or forehead thermometers can be less accurate in young infants — when in doubt, take a rectal temperature for the most reliable reading.

### Age Matters More Than the Number

How serious a fever is depends heavily on how old your child is:

- 
Under 3 months: Any fever (100.4°F or higher) is a medical emergency. Go to the ER immediately. Do not wait.
- 
3–6 months: Call your doctor right away, especially if the fever is 101°F or higher.
- 
6–24 months: Call your doctor if the fever reaches 102°F or has lasted more than 2 days.
- 
2 years and older: A fever is more concerning if it's very high (104°F+), lasts more than 3 days, or is accompanied by other worrying symptoms.

### Go to the ER or Call 911 If Your Child Has a Fever AND:

- 
Is under 3 months old
- 
Has a stiff neck or is unusually difficult to wake
- 
Has a purple or red rash that doesn't fade when pressed
- 
Is having trouble breathing
- 
Has a seizure

### How to Manage a Fever at Home (For Older Infants and Children)

For babies over 6 months and children, you can use children's acetaminophen or ibuprofen (ibuprofen is not recommended under 6 months) to manage fever and discomfort. Always dose by weight, not age. Keep your child hydrated — offer fluids frequently. Light clothing helps; don't bundle them up.
Fever itself is not the enemy. It's the body's way of fighting infection. The goal is comfort and monitoring, not necessarily bringing the temperature to normal.

### When in Doubt, Call Us

You know your baby. If something feels off — even if the temperature isn't sky-high — trust your gut and call. We would rather you reach out than worry alone.
Questions about your child's health? Call Burds Family Practice in Peosta at (563) 588-6659 or visit burdsfamilypractice.com to request an appointment. We're here for your family.

# Back-to-School & Sports Physicals in Peosta, IA

URL: https://www.burdsfamilypractice.com/blog/back-to-school-physicals-near-peosta-amp-dubuque-what-you-need-to-know.html

← Resources & Blog
Community Health Blog

## Back-to-School Physicals Near Peosta & Dubuque — What You Need to Know

Published Jul 27, 2026
2 min read
By Jennifer Burds, DNP, ARNP

August arrives fast, and suddenly everyone needs a physical. Whether your child needs a sports physical for fall athletics, a kindergarten entry exam, or just an annual well-child checkup before the school year, Burds Family Practice in Peosta is here to help local families get ready.

### What Is a School Physical?

A school or sports physical (also called a Pre-Participation Physical Evaluation, or PPE) checks your child's overall health and ensures they're ready for the demands of school and athletics. It typically includes:

- 
Height, weight, and BMI
- 
Blood pressure and heart rate
- 
Vision and hearing check
- 
Review of medical history and any chronic conditions
- 
Assessment of heart, lungs, abdomen, and musculoskeletal system
- 
For sports physicals: evaluation of any prior injuries, joint health, and fitness to play

### Is a Sports Physical the Same as a Well-Child Visit?

Not exactly. A sports physical is focused on clearing your child to play. A well-child visit is more comprehensive — it includes developmental screening, immunizations, and broader health counseling. If your child is due for both, we can often combine them into one visit. Just let us know when you schedule.

### What Vaccines Are Required for School in Iowa?

Iowa requires that children attending school be up to date on several vaccines, including DTaP, Polio, MMR, Varicella, and Hepatitis B, among others. We'll review your child's immunization records at the visit and administer any that are needed.

### When Should I Schedule?

Don't wait until the week before school starts. Our schedule fills up fast in July and August. We recommend booking your child's physical in June or July to make sure everything is in order before the first day of school — and to leave time for any follow-up if needed.

### Serving Peosta, Dubuque, and Surrounding Communities

Burds Family Practice is conveniently located in Peosta, Iowa — just minutes from Dubuque and the surrounding area. We welcome new patients of all ages and offer flexible scheduling for working families.
Questions about your child's health? Call Burds Family Practice in Peosta at (563) 588-6659 or visit burdsfamilypractice.com to request an appointment. We're here for your family.

# Car Seat Safety: A Stage-by-Stage Guide for Iowa Parents

URL: https://www.burdsfamilypractice.com/blog/car-seat-safety-a-stage-by-stage-guide-for-iowa-parents.html

← Resources & Blog
Community Health Blog

## Car Seat Safety: A Stage-by-Stage Guide for Iowa Parents

Published Sep 21, 2026
6 min read
By Jennifer Burds, DNP, ARNP

Nearly every parent has had the same quiet worry: Is this seat really installed right? Is my kid actually ready to move up? It's one of the most common questions we hear, and for good reason — the right seat, used the right way, is one of the single best things you can do to protect your child on the road.
Here's the part worth understanding up front: the law tells you the minimum, but the best-practice guidance tells you what's safest. Those aren't always the same thing. Let's walk through both.

### What Iowa law requires

Under Iowa's child restraint law (Iowa Code 321.446), at a minimum:

- 
Rear-facing for any child who is under 1 year old and under 20 pounds
- 
A child restraint system (car seat or booster), used per the manufacturer's instructions, through age 5 — until the sixth birthday
- 
Ages 6 through 17, a car seat, booster, or a properly fitted seat belt
A violation carries a scheduled fine of $135. But meeting the legal minimum isn't the same as doing what's safest, and the gap between the two is where a lot of avoidable injuries happen — a 9-month-old who has hit 21 pounds is no longer covered by Iowa's rear-facing requirement, and is still far safer rear-facing.

### The four stages, and how to know when to move up

The safest approach isn't tied to a birthday — it's tied to your child's size and the limits printed on your specific seat. The golden rule: keep your child in each stage until they reach the top height or weight limit of that seat, then move to the next. Every move “up” is actually a small step down in protection, so there's no rush.
Stage 1 — Rear-facing (infant/convertible seat)
Rear-facing is the safest position, especially for a young child's head, neck, and spine. Keep your child rear-facing as long as possible — until they hit the maximum height or weight your seat allows, which for many kids is well past age 2.
Stage 2 — Forward-facing with a harness
Once your child truly outgrows rear-facing, move to a forward-facing seat with a five-point harness. Use the harness (and top tether) until they reach that seat's limits.
Stage 3 — Booster seat
When they outgrow the harness, a belt-positioning booster raises them so the vehicle's seat belt lands correctly across the body. A booster must be used with both a lap and shoulder belt — never a lap belt alone.
Stage 4 — Seat belt alone
Your child is ready for the seat belt without a booster only when they pass the 5-step fit test below — often somewhere around 4'9″ and typically between ages 8 and 12.
And through all of it: kids under 13 are safest riding in the back seat.

### The 5-step fit test

Before you retire the booster, check all five:

- 
The child sits all the way back against the vehicle seat.
- 
Their knees bend comfortably at the edge of the seat.
- 
The lap belt sits low across the hips and upper thighs — not the belly.
- 
The shoulder belt crosses the middle of the chest and shoulder — not the neck or face.
- 
The child can sit like this, comfortably, for the whole ride.
If you can't check all five, they still need the booster. That's not being overprotective — that's the seat belt doing its job the way it was designed to.

### Common mistakes we see

Even great seats get used in ways that quietly reduce their protection. Watch for these:

- 
Chest clip too low. It should sit at armpit level, not down on the belly.
- 
A harness that's too loose. You shouldn't be able to pinch a fold of the strap at the shoulder.
- 
Bulky winter coats. Coats compress in a crash and leave the harness dangerously loose. Buckle your child in thin layers, then lay the coat or a blanket over the top.
- 
The front seat too soon. An active airbag can seriously injure a small child. Back seat until 13.
- 
A loose installation. The seat shouldn't move more than an inch side-to-side at the belt path.
- 
Expired or crash-involved seats. Car seats have expiration dates (usually printed on the seat), and any seat involved in a moderate or severe crash should be replaced.

### Get a free seat check

You don't have to guess. A Child Passenger Safety Technician (CPST) can check your installation and make sure your child is in the right stage — usually for free. Many hospitals, health departments, and fire stations in the area offer seat checks. If you're not sure where to start, ask us at your child's next visit and we'll point you in the right direction.
Car seats are one of those things where a five-minute check buys a lot of peace of mind. We're glad to be part of that for your family — the same way we are with poison and medication safety at home.
Questions about your child's seat or ready to schedule a visit? Call Burds Family Practice in Peosta at (563) 588-6659, or send us a message to request an appointment. You can see everything we offer on our services page.

### Frequently asked questions

#### What is Iowa's car seat law?

At a minimum, Iowa requires a rear-facing seat for a child who is under 1 year old and under 20 pounds, a child restraint system through age 5, and a car seat, booster, or seat belt from ages 6 through 17. Best-practice guidance goes further than the legal minimum.

#### When can my child stop using a booster seat?

When they pass the 5-step fit test — sitting back against the seat with knees bent at the edge, the lap belt low on the hips, and the shoulder belt across the chest — usually around 4'9″ and often between ages 8 and 12.

#### How long should my child ride rear-facing?

As long as possible — until they reach the maximum height or weight limit of their rear-facing seat, which for many children is well beyond age 2. Iowa's legal minimum is much lower than what's safest.

#### Is it safe to buckle my child in with a winter coat on?

No. A bulky coat compresses in a crash and leaves the harness too loose. Buckle your child in thin layers, then place the coat or a blanket over the harness.

#### Where can I get my car seat checked in the Dubuque area?

A Child Passenger Safety Technician can check it, often for free, through local hospitals, health departments, or fire stations. Ask us at your next visit and we'll help you find one.

# DOT Physicals in the Dubuque Area

URL: https://www.burdsfamilypractice.com/blog/dot-physicals-in-the-dubuque-area-what-to-expect-and-what-to-bring.html

← Resources & Blog
Community Health Blog

## DOT Physicals in the Dubuque Area: What to Expect and What to Bring

Published Sep 7, 2026
4 min read
By Jennifer Burds, DNP, ARNP

If your job depends on your license, your DOT physical shouldn't be a hassle. For a lot of drivers, it's a once-every-two-years errand that gets squeezed in between loads — so the last thing you need is a long wait, a confusing form, or a return trip because you forgot a piece of paper.
At Burds Family Practice, we do these exams the way we'd want them done for our own families: on time, explained plainly, and handled by a certified medical examiner. Here's exactly what to know before you come in.

### Who needs a DOT physical?

If you drive commercially, you probably do. That includes most CDL holders and certain non-CDL commercial operations. If you're not sure whether your role requires one, your employer's safety manager will know — and you're welcome to call us and ask.
The exam has to be performed by a medical examiner listed on the FMCSA National Registry. Not every clinic has one on staff. We do, which is part of why local drivers and employers come to us instead of driving out of the metro.

### What actually happens during the exam

A DOT physical is a focused check that you're medically fit to operate safely. It usually takes about 20 to 30 minutes and includes:

- 
Vision — measured with or without glasses or contacts, plus a check of your field of vision and color recognition
- 
Hearing — a basic check to confirm you can hear well enough to drive safely
- 
Blood pressure and pulse
- 
A urine screen — this checks for things like protein or sugar as a health screen; it is not a drug test
- 
A physical exam — heart, lungs, abdomen, reflexes, and a review of your health history
Most drivers walk out with a medical certificate good for up to 24 months. If you have a condition we want to keep an eye on — say, blood pressure that's a little high — the examiner may issue a shorter certificate so we can recheck sooner. That's not a punishment; it's how we keep you certified and on the road.

### What to bring

This is where a little prep saves you a second trip. Please bring:

- 
A photo ID
- 
A list of your current medications — names, doses, and who prescribes them
- 
Your glasses, contacts, or hearing aids if you use them
- 
Paperwork for any managed conditions, such as:

- 
Diabetes: recent blood sugar or A1c results
- 
Heart conditions: a note or records from your cardiologist
- 
Sleep apnea: your CPAP compliance report
- 
Vision or hearing: any specialist forms you've been given
- 
Any prior FMCSA exemption or variance paperwork, if you have one
If you're managing a health condition, the more current your records, the smoother the visit. When a driver shows up with the right paperwork, we can usually certify same-day.

### A word on drug and alcohol testing

The DOT physical and DOT drug/alcohol testing are two different things, though employers often schedule them together. If your company needs both, we can coordinate that in one visit so your driver isn't making two trips. Employers, that's worth a conversation — we'll get to that below.

### Local drivers, local clinic

We're a family practice in the Peosta, Dyersville, and Dubuque area, which means you're not just a name on a certificate. If your physical turns up something worth a closer look, you're already sitting in a clinic that can help you sort it out — often the same day — instead of sending you off to start over somewhere else.
Ready to schedule? Call Burds Family Practice at (563) 588-6659, or send us a message to request an appointment. Fleet or multiple drivers? See our full occupational health services for employers — we'll set up a schedule that works around your operation.

### Frequently asked questions

#### How long is a DOT physical good for?

Up to 24 months. If you have a health condition we want to monitor, your examiner may issue a certificate for a shorter period.

#### Is the DOT physical a drug test?

No. The urine screen during a DOT physical checks for health markers, not drugs. Drug and alcohol testing is separate, though it can often be done at the same appointment.

#### What should I bring to my DOT physical?

A photo ID, a list of your current medications, your glasses, contacts, or hearing aids if you use them, and records for any managed conditions like diabetes, heart issues, or sleep apnea.

#### Do I need an appointment?

We recommend booking ahead so we can have your certified medical examiner ready and get you in and out quickly. Call (563) 588-6659 or send us a message to schedule.

# How to Tell If Your Child Has Strep Throat | Symptoms

URL: https://www.burdsfamilypractice.com/blog/how-do-i-know-if-my-child-has-strep-throat.html

← Resources & Blog
Community Health Blog

## How Do I Know If My Child Has Strep Throat?

Published Jun 29, 2026
2 min read
By Jennifer Burds, DNP, ARNP

Every parent dreads the words: "My throat hurts." Sore throats are incredibly common in kids, but most are caused by viruses and will clear up on their own. Strep throat is different — it's a bacterial infection that needs antibiotics to treat. The tricky part? It doesn't always look the way you'd expect.

### Strep vs. Regular Sore Throat: What's the Difference?

Strep throat (caused by Group A Streptococcus bacteria) tends to come on suddenly and without the usual cold symptoms. Here's how it often compares:

- 
Strep: Sudden sore throat, fever, painful swallowing, swollen lymph nodes, sometimes red spots or white patches in the throat
- 
Viral sore throat: Gradual onset, usually comes with runny nose, cough, or congestion
Important: you cannot diagnose strep by looking at the throat alone. A rapid strep test at your provider's office is the only reliable way to know for sure.

### Symptoms to Watch For

- 
Sore throat that comes on quickly
- 
Fever of 101°F or higher
- 
Painful or difficult swallowing
- 
Red, swollen tonsils (sometimes with white streaks or patches)
- 
Swollen, tender lymph nodes in the neck
- 
Stomachache, headache, or nausea (especially in younger kids)
- 
A red rash that feels like sandpaper (this may indicate scarlet fever, caused by the same bacteria)

### What Happens If Strep Goes Untreated?

Untreated strep can lead to complications including rheumatic fever, which can damage the heart, and kidney problems. This is why it's important not to wait it out if you suspect strep — especially if symptoms are not improving after a couple of days.

### Treatment

If the strep test is positive, we'll prescribe a course of antibiotics. It's essential that your child finishes the entire prescription, even if they start feeling better quickly. Your child can return to school or daycare 24 hours after starting antibiotics and once they're fever-free.
Questions about your child's health? Call Burds Family Practice in Peosta at (563) 588-6659 or visit burdsfamilypractice.com to request an appointment. We're here for your family.

# Child Ear Infection: Symptoms & What to Do | Peosta IA

URL: https://www.burdsfamilypractice.com/blog/my-child-has-an-ear-infection-what-should-i-do.html

← Resources & Blog
Community Health Blog

## My Child Has an Ear Infection — What Should I Do?

Published Jun 15, 2026
2 min read
By Jennifer Burds, DNP, ARNP

It's 9 p.m. Your child is crying, tugging at their ear, and running a fever. Sound familiar? Ear infections are one of the most common reasons parents in the Peosta and Dubuque area bring their kids in to see us — and for good reason. They're painful, they come on fast, and it can be hard to know what to do.
Here's what you need to know.

### Signs Your Child Has an Ear Infection

Ear infections don't always announce themselves clearly, especially in babies and toddlers who can't tell you what hurts. Watch for:

- 
Tugging or pulling at one or both ears
- 
Fussiness or crying more than usual
- 
Trouble sleeping
- 
Fever (often above 100°F)
- 
Fluid draining from the ear
- 
Trouble hearing or responding to sounds
- 
Balance problems or seeming clumsier than normal

### Can an Ear Infection Go Away on Its Own?

Sometimes, yes. Mild ear infections in older children (ages 2 and up) can resolve without antibiotics within a few days. However, in infants under 6 months or any child with severe symptoms, antibiotics are usually needed.
The safest approach? Call your child's provider and let them make the call. Waiting too long to seek treatment for a true bacterial infection can lead to complications.

### When to Call the Doctor Right Away

- 
Your child is under 6 months old
- 
Fever is 102°F or higher
- 
Symptoms are getting worse after 2–3 days
- 
There is fluid or pus draining from the ear
- 
Your child seems in significant pain

### What to Do While You Wait for the Appointment

A warm (not hot) compress held gently against the ear can ease pain. Over-the-counter pain relievers like children's acetaminophen or ibuprofen (for children over 6 months) can also help with discomfort and fever. Always follow dosing instructions for your child's weight and age.

### Can Ear Infections Be Prevented?

Not entirely, but a few things help: keeping your child's vaccinations up to date (including the flu vaccine), avoiding secondhand smoke, and breastfeeding if possible. If your child gets ear infections frequently, we can talk through longer-term options, including whether a referral to an ENT is right for them.
Questions about your child's health? Call Burds Family Practice in Peosta at (563) 588-6659 or visit burdsfamilypractice.com to request an appointment. We're here for your family.

# Occupational Health for Local Employers

## Occupational Health for Local Employers: Keeping Your Team Safe and Working

Published Oct 5, 2026
4 min read
By Jennifer Burds, DNP, ARNP

When an employee gets hurt on the job, the clock starts. Every hour that person spends figuring out where to go, sitting in an unfamiliar ER, or waiting for someone to call you back is an hour of lost work, mounting cost, and unnecessary stress — for them and for you.
It doesn't have to work that way. A good occupational health partner turns those moments from a scramble into a routine. At Burds Family Practice, we work with employers across the Peosta, Dyersville, and Dubuque area to keep teams healthy, compliant, and on the clock.

### Why partner with a local family practice for occ health

Plenty of employers default to sending workers to the emergency room or a distant urgent care. It's understandable — but it's often the most expensive, slowest, and least coordinated option available.
Working with a local clinic changes the math:

- 
Your people are seen by someone who knows your business, not a rotating cast of strangers
- 
Care is coordinated — the same clinic that handles the pre-employment physical can handle the injury, the follow-up, and the return-to-work clearance
- 
You get a real point of contact instead of a phone tree
- 
It's close — less time off the floor, faster answers, fewer surprises
That continuity matters most when something goes wrong. The provider treating an injured worker already has context, and can move quickly toward the goal everyone shares: getting that person healthy and back to work safely.

### What we handle for employers

We build occupational health around what actually shows up in a working business:
Pre-employment and compliance exams

- 
Pre-employment physicals
- 
DOT physicals from a certified medical examiner
- 
Fit-for-duty and return-to-work evaluations
- 
Vision and hearing screenings
Drug and alcohol screening

- 
Pre-employment, random, post-accident, and reasonable-suspicion testing
- 
Coordinated with DOT exams when both are needed, so drivers make one trip
Work injury care

- 
Prompt evaluation and treatment of on-the-job injuries
- 
Coordination with your workers' compensation process
- 
Clear, timely documentation for your records
Return-to-work and prevention

- 
Return-to-work clearances with realistic work restrictions
- 
Guidance on light-duty options so you can keep people contributing while they heal
- 
Injury-prevention conversations before problems start

### The part employers underestimate: return-to-work

The most expensive stretch of any workplace injury is often the gap between “hurt” and “back to work.” Vague restrictions, slow paperwork, and no plan can turn a minor injury into weeks of lost productivity.
We treat return-to-work as part of the treatment, not an afterthought. That means clear restrictions you can actually staff around, honest timelines, and documentation that lands when you need it. Often the best outcome isn't full time off — it's a thoughtful light-duty plan that keeps a valued employee engaged while they recover.

### Built for the way local businesses actually run

You don't need a big corporate contract to get organized occupational health. Whether you've got five employees or fifty, we can set up a straightforward arrangement — scheduled physicals, on-call injury care, coordinated screening — that fits your operation and your budget.
We're independently owned and rooted right here in western Dubuque County. That's how we approach the employers who keep this area running: as neighbors, not accounts.
Let's talk. Call (563) 588-6659 or email bfpstaff@burdsfamilypractice.com to set up a short conversation about what your team needs. You can also see our full occupational health services for employers. We'll build something practical, not a binder full of services you'll never use.

### Frequently asked questions

#### What does an occupational health provider do?

An occupational health provider handles the health side of employment — pre-employment and DOT physicals, drug and alcohol screening, on-the-job injury care, and return-to-work clearances — coordinated in one place.

#### Is it cheaper than sending injured workers to the ER?

In most cases, yes. Routine work injuries treated in a clinic setting are typically faster and less costly than an emergency room visit, and the coordinated follow-up helps employees return to work sooner.

#### Do you work with small businesses?

Yes. We set up occupational health arrangements that fit businesses of all sizes across the Peosta, Dyersville, and Dubuque area.

#### Can you handle DOT physicals and drug screening in one visit?

Yes. When a driver needs both, we coordinate them in a single appointment to save time.

# Outdoor Safety for Kids: Bikes, ATVs & UTVs in Rural Iowa

URL: https://www.burdsfamilypractice.com/blog/outdoor-safety-for-kids-bikes-atvs-and-utvs-in-rural-iowa.html

← Resources & Blog
Community Health Blog

## Outdoor Safety for Kids: Bikes, ATVs, and UTVs in Rural Iowa

Published Oct 19, 2026
6 min read
By Jennifer Burds, DNP, ARNP

Around here, kids grow up outside. Bikes down the lane, a four-wheeler for chores, the side-by-side loaded up for a ride around the property — it's part of life in this part of Iowa, and it should be. But the same machines that make farm and country life fun are also behind some of the most serious injuries we see in kids.
The goal isn't to keep kids off wheels. It's to make sure they come home in one piece. Here's how.

### Start with the one non-negotiable: helmets

If there's a single habit worth being stubborn about, it's this one. A helmet is the difference between a scary story and a tragedy in a huge share of head injuries.
A few things to get right:

- 
Fit matters as much as wearing it. The helmet should sit level, low on the forehead — about two finger-widths above the eyebrows — snug enough that it doesn't shift when your child shakes their head. The straps should form a “V” under each ear and buckle snug under the chin.
- 
Match the helmet to the machine. A bike helmet is fine for bikes and scooters. For an ATV or UTV, use a DOT-approved motorcycle-style helmet — bike helmets aren't built for motorized speeds.
- 
Replace a helmet after any real crash, even if it looks fine. Its job is to absorb one big hit.
- 
Kids copy adults. If you wear yours, they'll wear theirs. That's the whole trick.

### Bikes and scooters

Biking is one of the healthiest things a kid can do — a little setup keeps it safe:

- 
Right-sized bike. Your child should be able to plant their feet and stop confidently. A too-big bike they'll “grow into” is harder to control now.
- 
Be seen. Bright clothing, reflectors, and lights at dusk. On gravel and county roads, drivers aren't always expecting a kid on a bike.
- 
Know the rules of the road. Ride with traffic, stop at intersections, use hand signals, and walk the bike across busy crossings.
- 
Watch the driveway and the ditch. A lot of close calls happen right at home, backing out or pulling in. Teach kids where it's safe to ride and where it isn't.

### ATVs and UTVs: the rural reality

This is the big one, and it deserves straight talk. ATVs and side-by-sides are powerful, top-heavy, and unforgiving of a small mistake — and children simply don't have the size, strength, or judgment to handle them the way an adult can.
What Iowa law says. The rules depend on where you're riding:

- 
On public roads, the driver must be 18 or older with a valid driver's license. Kids can't legally drive an ATV or UTV on the road.
- 
On public land, public ice, and designated riding areas and trails, riders ages 12–17 must carry a DNR-approved ATV education certificate. Children under 12 must be under the direct supervision of a parent or guardian who is at least 18, experienced in ATV operation, and holds a valid driver's license — meaning visual and verbal contact at all times.
- 
At Iowa's designated OHV riding areas, helmets are required for every operator and passenger, at any age — including in the parking and loading areas.
- 
On your own private land — where most farm kids actually ride — those specific age rules don't apply the same way. That's exactly why the safety decisions fall to you.
What the doctors recommend — beyond the law. Pediatric safety experts are clear that children under 16 shouldn't operate adult-size ATVs, and that most youth ATV deaths and injuries are preventable with the right limits. So a few family rules worth holding firm on:

- 
Match the machine to the rider. A child on an adult-size ATV is the single biggest risk factor. Youth models exist for a reason.
- 
No passengers on a single-rider ATV. Ever. They're designed for one person, and a passenger makes them far harder to control.
- 
In a UTV, everyone buckles up and stays inside the roll cage — arms, legs, and heads in, no more riders than there are seats.
- 
Supervise anyone under 16, and don't hand over the keys until a child has the size and maturity to match the machine.
- 
A safety course is worth it even when it isn't required. The Iowa DNR offers ATV education, and the habits stick.
- 
Sober, seated, and slow to start. No alcohol, no overloading, and let new riders build skill on flat, familiar ground before anything steep or fast.
None of this means the four-wheeler has to sit in the shed. It means the ride is set up so a bad moment stays a scare instead of a hospital trip.

### Why we're bringing this up

We love that kids here grow up capable and outdoors — it's one of the best things about raising a family in this area. We just see, up close, what happens when a helmet gets skipped or a kid ends up on a machine that's too much for them. A few simple rules prevent the large majority of it.
If you want to talk through what's age-appropriate for your child — which bike, whether they're ready for a youth ATV, what gear actually matters — bring it up at their next visit. That's exactly the kind of question we're here for, right alongside car seat safety.
Ready to schedule a well-child visit or have a safety question? Call Burds Family Practice in Peosta at (563) 588-6659, or send us a message to request an appointment. You can see everything we offer on our services page.

### Frequently asked questions

#### How old do you have to be to drive an ATV or UTV in Iowa?

On public roads, the driver must be at least 18 with a valid license. On public land, public ice, and designated riding areas and trails, riders 12–17 need a DNR ATV education certificate, and those under 12 must be directly supervised by an experienced, licensed adult. At designated OHV riding areas, helmets are required for everyone regardless of age. On private land, these specific rules don't apply the same way, so families set their own limits.

#### Should young kids ride adult-size ATVs?

No. Pediatric safety experts recommend that children under 16 not operate adult-size ATVs. Riding an adult machine is the biggest risk factor for youth ATV injuries — use age-appropriate youth models instead.

#### Can my child ride as a passenger on a four-wheeler?

Not on a single-rider ATV — they're designed for one person, and a passenger makes them much harder to control safely. In a UTV, every rider should be belted, inside the roll cage, with no more riders than seats.

#### What kind of helmet does my child need for an ATV?

A DOT-approved motorcycle-style helmet, not a bicycle helmet. Bike helmets aren't rated for motorized speeds. For bikes and scooters, a properly fitted bike helmet is right.

#### Does Iowa require kids to wear bike helmets?

Iowa has no statewide bicycle helmet law, though some cities may have local rules. Regardless of the law, a properly fitted helmet is strongly recommended every ride.

# Poison & Medication Safety at Home for Kids

URL: https://www.burdsfamilypractice.com/blog/poison-and-medication-safety-at-home-protecting-your-kids.html

← Resources & Blog
Community Health Blog

## Poison and Medication Safety at Home: Protecting Your Kids

Published Aug 24, 2026
5 min read
By Jennifer Burds, DNP, ARNP

Most accidental poisonings don't happen in dramatic ways. They happen in ordinary moments — a purse left on the couch, a pill that rolled under the counter, a bottle of gummy vitamins that looks a lot like candy to a two-year-old. The good news is that the same everyday awareness that prevents most of them is easy to build into your routine.
Here's a straightforward guide to keeping the little ones in your home safe, plus what to do if something does happen.

### Save this number now

Before anything else, put the Poison Help line — 1-800-222-1222 — in your phone, and post it on the fridge. It's free, available 24 hours a day, and staffed by experts who can tell you in minutes whether you're dealing with an emergency or a non-issue.
Program it in every caregiver's phone: both parents, grandparents, the babysitter. When something happens, you don't want to be searching for a number.

### Store medicine up, away, and locked

Medications are the most common cause of childhood poisoning, and it's often the ones we don't think of as dangerous — vitamins, iron supplements, and adult prescriptions a child gets into.

- 
Keep all medicine up and away — out of sight and out of reach, ideally in a locked or latched cabinet
- 
Store everything in its original child-resistant container, and relock the cap every single time. Remember: child-resistant is not childproof. It buys time; it isn't a guarantee.
- 
Never call medicine "candy" to get a reluctant kid to take it. Kids remember.
- 
Be extra careful with gummy vitamins and supplements — they look exactly like the treats children are told they can have
- 
Watch the in-between moments: pills in a purse, a nightstand, a coat pocket, or a pill organizer on the counter are among the most common ways kids get into medication

### The household dangers parents overlook

Medicine isn't the only risk. A few items send more kids to the ER than most parents expect:

- 
Button batteries — the small coin-shaped batteries in remotes, key fobs, greeting cards, and toys. Swallowed, they can cause serious internal burns within hours. Keep battery compartments taped shut and loose batteries locked away, and treat a suspected swallow as an emergency.
- 
High-powered magnets — the tiny, shiny "desk toy" magnets. If a child swallows more than one, they can pinch the intestines together. Keep them out of any home with young kids.
- 
Laundry and dishwasher pods — bright, squishy, and exactly the size of something a toddler wants to bite
- 
Cleaning products — store them high, never under the sink, and never transfer them into unlabeled cups or bottles
- 
Liquid nicotine and vape products — even small amounts are dangerous to children
- 
Cannabis edibles — often packaged to look like ordinary candy or snacks; lock them away as you would any medication
- 
Essential oils and antifreeze — both can be harmful in small amounts, and antifreeze tastes sweet

### Don't forget other homes

Grandparents' houses, a friend's home, the cabin — these often aren't childproofed, and they're where daily medications tend to sit out on counters and nightstands. Before your child spends time somewhere new, take two minutes to look around at their eye level. It's the fastest way to spot what needs to move.

### If you think your child got into something

Stay calm, and act based on what you're seeing:

- 
If your child is unconscious, not breathing, having a seizure, or struggling to breathe — call 911 immediately.
- 
If your child is awake and alert but you think they swallowed, touched, or inhaled something they shouldn't have — call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222 right away. They'll walk you through exactly what to do.
A few important don'ts: don't wait for symptoms to appear before calling, don't try to make your child vomit, and don't use ipecac syrup — older advice that's no longer recommended. Let the experts guide you.

### Clean out what you don't need

The safest medication is the one that isn't in your house anymore. Every so often, go through your cabinets and safely dispose of expired or unused medicines — many pharmacies and local law enforcement offices offer take-back drop boxes. Fewer bottles around means fewer chances for a curious kid to find one.

### We're here for the questions, big and small

Childproofing can feel like a moving target as your kids grow. If you're not sure what to lock up, what to worry about, or what to do about a specific product in your home, ask us at your child's next visit — whether that's a well-child checkup, a back-to-school or sports physical, or a sick visit. That's exactly the kind of thing your family practice is for.
Have a pediatric care question or need to schedule a visit? Call Burds Family Practice in Peosta at (563) 588-6659, or send us a message to request an appointment. See everything we offer on our services page.
This article is for general education and isn't a substitute for medical advice. In an emergency, call 911 or the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222.

### Frequently asked questions

#### What is the Poison Control number?

The national Poison Help line is 1-800-222-1222. It's free, confidential, available 24/7, and staffed by experts. Save it in your phone and post it at home.

#### What are the most common causes of child poisoning at home?

Medications — including vitamins, supplements, and adult prescriptions — are the most common. Other frequent culprits include cleaning products, laundry pods, button batteries, liquid nicotine, and cannabis edibles.

#### Should I make my child vomit if they swallow something?

No. Do not try to induce vomiting or use ipecac syrup. Call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222 or 911 and follow their guidance.

#### Why are button batteries so dangerous?

If swallowed, a button battery can cause serious internal burns within hours. Keep battery compartments secured and treat a suspected swallow as an emergency — call 911 or Poison Control right away.

#### How should I store medicine with young kids in the house?

Keep all medicine up, away, and out of sight — ideally locked. Use original child-resistant containers, relock caps every time, and never refer to medicine as candy.

# Pink Eye in Kids: Signs & When to Call the Doctor

URL: https://www.burdsfamilypractice.com/blog/signs-of-pink-eye-in-kids-and-when-to-call-the-doctor.html

← Resources & Blog
Community Health Blog

## Signs of Pink Eye in Kids — And When to Call the Doctor

Published Jul 20, 2026
2 min read
By Jennifer Burds, DNP, ARNP

Pink eye (conjunctivitis) spreads fast in schools and daycares, and it can look scary even when it's not serious. The good news: most cases in kids are mild and treatable. Here's how to tell what type your child has and what to do about it.

### What Does Pink Eye Look Like?

The telltale sign is redness in the white of one or both eyes. But the other symptoms vary depending on the cause:

- 
Bacterial pink eye: Yellow or green discharge, often causing the eyelashes to crust together overnight. Usually starts in one eye and can spread to the other.
- 
Viral pink eye: Watery discharge, often accompanying a cold or respiratory illness. Very contagious.
- 
Allergic pink eye: Itchy, watery eyes in both eyes at once. Often comes with sneezing or a runny nose. Not contagious.

### Does Pink Eye Always Need Antibiotics?

No — and this surprises a lot of parents. Viral and allergic pink eye don't respond to antibiotics at all. Only bacterial pink eye is treated with antibiotic eye drops. Since it's hard to tell the types apart without an exam, it's worth bringing your child in so we can make the right call.

### When to Call the Doctor

- 
Discharge is yellow or green
- 
Eye is very swollen or the eyelid is puffy
- 
Your child is complaining of eye pain (not just irritation)
- 
Vision seems blurry or affected
- 
Symptoms are not improving after a few days
- 
Your newborn has any eye discharge — this always warrants a call

### Keeping It From Spreading

Pink eye is highly contagious. Keep your child home from school until they've been on antibiotic drops for at least 24 hours (for bacterial) or until the discharge clears (for viral). Frequent handwashing is the best prevention — teach kids not to touch their eyes and to wash hands often, especially at school.
Questions about your child's health? Call Burds Family Practice in Peosta at (563) 588-6659 or visit burdsfamilypractice.com to request an appointment. We're here for your family.

# What Is Direct Primary Care? | Burds Family Practice Peosta, IA Meta

URL: https://www.burdsfamilypractice.com/blog/what-is-direct-primary-care-and-why-peosta-families-love-it.html

## What Is Direct Primary Care — And Why Peosta Families Love It

Published May 16, 2026
8 min read
By Jennifer Burds, DNP, ARNP

If you've ever sat in a waiting room for 45 minutes only to spend 7 minutes with your doctor, you already understand why so many people are frustrated with traditional healthcare. There's a better way — and it's called Direct Primary Care (DPC).
At Burds Family Practice in Peosta, Iowa, we offer Direct Primary Care as an alternative (or complement) to traditional insurance-based visits. Here's everything you need to know.

#### So, What Exactly Is Direct Primary Care?

Direct Primary Care is a straightforward healthcare model: you pay a flat monthly membership fee, and in return, you get unlimited access to your primary care provider — no copays, no surprise bills, no insurance middleman.
Think of it like a gym membership, but instead of access to a treadmill, you get access to your healthcare team.

#### What's Included in a DPC Membership at Burds Family Practice?

With our DPC membership, patients enjoy:

- 
Unlimited visits — as many as you need, no extra charge
- 
Same-day or next-day appointments — no waiting weeks to be seen
- 
Direct access to your provider — call, text, or message us directly
- 
Longer appointment times — we actually get to know you
- 
Preventive care and chronic disease management
- 
No insurance required — though you can still use insurance for specialists or hospital care

#### Who Is DPC Right For?

Direct Primary Care is a great fit if you:

- 
Are self-employed or your employer doesn't offer health insurance
- 
Have a high-deductible insurance plan and want affordable day-to-day care
- 
Are tired of rushed appointments and want a real relationship with your provider
- 
Have a chronic condition that requires frequent check-ins
- 
Simply want more personalized, attentive healthcare for your family

#### How Much Does It Cost?

DPC is designed to be affordable. Instead of paying per visit — which adds up fast — you pay one predictable monthly fee. Many patients find they actually save money compared to traditional copays and deductibles, especially if they visit the doctor more than once or twice a year.

#### Why Patients Choose Burds Family Practice for DPC

At Burds Family Practice, we believe healthcare should feel like a relationship, not a transaction. Our team, led by Jenny Burds, FNP, has over 25 years of healthcare experience and a deep commitment to this community. When you're a DPC member, you're not just a chart number — you're family.
Ready to learn more? Give us a call at (563) 588-6659 or visit us at 8411 Peosta Commercial Ct Suite #8, Peosta, IA. We'd love to walk you through our membership options and find the right fit for you and your family.
Burds Family Practice serves patients in Peosta, Dubuque, Asbury, Cascade, and surrounding communities in Northeast Iowa.

### Blog Post 2

## Semaglutide vs. Tirzepatide: Which Medical Weight Loss Medication Is Right for You?

Meta Title: Semaglutide vs Tirzepatide for Weight Loss | Burds Family Practice Peosta, IA Meta Description: Semaglutide (Wegovy) or tirzepatide (Zepbound) — which is right for you? Our team at Burds Family Practice in Peosta, IA breaks down both options to help you decide. Target Keywords: semaglutide Peosta Iowa, tirzepatide Dubuque area, medical weight loss Iowa, Wegovy Zepbound family practice
Medical weight loss has changed dramatically in the last few years. If you've been hearing a lot about medications like Wegovy and Zepbound, you're not alone — these treatments have helped thousands of people achieve meaningful, lasting weight loss. But with two strong options on the table, how do you know which one is right for you?
At Burds Family Practice in Peosta, Iowa, we offer both semaglutide (Wegovy) and tirzepatide (Zepbound) as part of our medical weight loss program. Here's a friendly breakdown to help you understand the difference.

#### First, How Do These Medications Work?

Both medications work by targeting hormones in your body that regulate hunger and blood sugar. In simple terms, they help you feel fuller faster and for longer — which naturally leads to eating less and losing weight over time.

- 
Semaglutide (Wegovy) targets one hormone receptor: GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1)
- 
Tirzepatide (Zepbound) targets two hormone receptors: GLP-1 and GIP (glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide)
Because tirzepatide works on two receptors instead of one, clinical studies have shown it tends to produce slightly greater weight loss on average — but both are highly effective.

#### Semaglutide (Wegovy): What to Know

Semaglutide has been around a bit longer and has a well-established track record. It's given as a weekly injection and has been shown to help patients lose a significant percentage of their body weight when combined with healthy lifestyle changes.
Good fit if you:

- 
Want a proven, well-studied option
- 
Are managing Type 2 diabetes alongside weight loss
- 
Prefer to start with a single-receptor medication

#### Tirzepatide (Zepbound): What to Know

Tirzepatide is newer and has shown impressive results in clinical trials — in some studies, patients lost up to 20–22% of their body weight. Like semaglutide, it's a weekly injection.
Good fit if you:

- 
Want the option with the highest average weight loss results
- 
Haven't had success with other weight loss approaches
- 
Are looking for a dual-action medication

#### Common Side Effects for Both

Both medications can cause similar side effects, especially when you're first starting out. The most common include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and constipation. These usually improve as your body adjusts. Starting at a low dose and gradually increasing helps minimize discomfort.

#### Which One Should You Choose?

Here's the honest answer: it depends on your individual health history, goals, and how your body responds. That's exactly why medical supervision matters. At Burds Family Practice, we'll review your health history, discuss your goals, and help you figure out which option makes the most sense for you — and monitor your progress every step of the way.
Weight loss medication isn't a magic fix, but paired with lifestyle changes and the right medical support, it can be a powerful tool.
Interested in learning more about our medical weight loss program? Call us at (563) 588-6659 or stop by our office in Peosta. We're here to help you take that next step with confidence.

Note: This blog post is for educational purposes only and is not a substitute for personalized medical advice. Please consult with a healthcare provider before starting any weight loss medication.
Burds Family Practice serves patients in Peosta, Dubuque, Asbury, Cascade, and surrounding communities in Northeast Iowa.

### Blog Post 3

## Why Choose a Nurse Practitioner for Your Primary Care?

Meta Title: Why See a Nurse Practitioner for Primary Care? | Burds Family Practice Peosta Meta Description: Nurse practitioners offer expert, personalized primary care. Learn why patients across Peosta and the Dubuque area trust the NPs at Burds Family Practice for their family's health. Target Keywords: nurse practitioner primary care Iowa, NP family doctor Peosta, family nurse practitioner Dubuque area, primary care provider Peosta IA
When most people think of going to the doctor, they picture an MD in a white coat. But here's something worth knowing: nurse practitioners (NPs) are highly trained, fully licensed healthcare providers who deliver excellent primary care — and for many patients, they're actually the preferred choice.
At Burds Family Practice, our care is led by Jenny Burds, FNP, a family nurse practitioner with over 25 years of healthcare experience. Here's why so many families in Peosta and the surrounding Dubuque area choose an NP for their primary care.

#### What Is a Nurse Practitioner?

A nurse practitioner is an advanced practice registered nurse (APRN) with a master's or doctoral degree in nursing. NPs complete thousands of hours of clinical training and are licensed to:

- 
Diagnose and treat acute and chronic conditions
- 
Order and interpret lab work and diagnostic tests
- 
Prescribe medications
- 
Provide preventive care and health counseling
- 
Manage complex, ongoing health conditions
In Iowa, nurse practitioners are able to practice and prescribe independently — meaning you receive comprehensive, expert care.

#### NPs Are Known for Spending More Time with Patients

One of the most common things patients say when they switch to an NP-led practice is: "I finally feel heard."
Nurse practitioners are trained with a strong emphasis on the whole person — not just the diagnosis. They tend to spend more time during appointments, ask about lifestyle factors, stress, and family history, and take a collaborative approach to your care. It's medicine that treats you as a person, not just a set of symptoms.

#### The Education and Experience Behind the Care

Jenny Burds earned her degree from Clarke University and has spent over a decade as a nurse practitioner — plus more than 15 years in other healthcare roles before that. Our team also includes Channah, a Doctor of Nursing Practice (DNP) graduate from Clarke University who brings 8+ years of nursing experience.
That depth of knowledge and genuine passion for patient care is what sets Burds Family Practice apart.

#### NPs Offer Continuity of Care

At larger health systems, you might see a different provider every single visit. At Burds Family Practice, you build a real relationship with your care team. That continuity means your provider knows your history, notices changes over time, and catches things that might otherwise slip through the cracks.

#### Still Have Questions About Seeing an NP?

That's completely normal! Many people haven't had an NP as their primary care provider before. We're happy to answer any questions you have about our training, our practice model, or what to expect at your first visit.
The bottom line: great primary care isn't about a title — it's about a provider who knows you, listens to you, and genuinely cares about your health. That's what we're here for.
Call us at (563) 588-6659 or visit burdsfamilypractice.com to book your first appointment. New patients are always welcome.

# Vaccines at Your Child's 4-Year Checkup | Peosta IA

URL: https://www.burdsfamilypractice.com/blog/what-vaccines-does-my-child-need-at-their-4-year-checkup.html

← Resources & Blog
Community Health Blog

## What Vaccines Does My Child Need at Their 4-Year Checkup?

Published Jul 13, 2026
2 min read
By Jennifer Burds, DNP, ARNP

The 4-year well-child visit is one of the most important checkups in early childhood. It happens right before most kids start kindergarten, and it includes several key vaccines that will protect them through the school years. Here's what to expect.

### Vaccines Typically Given at Age 4

At the 4-year visit, the CDC and American Academy of Pediatrics recommend the following vaccines (these are booster doses of vaccines your child started as an infant):

- 
DTaP — Protects against diphtheria, tetanus, and whooping cough (pertussis)
- 
IPV — Protects against polio
- 
MMR — Protects against measles, mumps, and rubella
- 
Varicella — Protects against chickenpox
Your child may also receive the flu vaccine if it's flu season or if they're due for their annual shot.

### What Else Happens at the 4-Year Visit?

Beyond vaccines, the 4-year checkup includes a lot:

- 
Height, weight, and BMI check
- 
Blood pressure measurement
- 
Vision and hearing screening
- 
Developmental assessment — talking, social skills, motor abilities
- 
Questions about school readiness, sleep, screen time, and behavior
- 
A chance for you to bring up any concerns before kindergarten

### Is My Child Required to Have These Vaccines to Start Kindergarten?

In Iowa, children are required to have certain vaccines to attend school, though medical and religious exemptions exist. Getting your child up to date before the school year starts makes the transition much smoother — and protects classmates who can't be vaccinated for medical reasons.

### My Child Is Nervous About Shots. Any Tips?

This is very common. Be honest with your child — don't say it won't hurt at all, but do reassure them it will be quick. Bring a comfort item. Let them know it's okay to cry. And plan something fun for afterward. Our team is great with nervous kids — we'll go at their pace.
Questions about your child's health? Call Burds Family Practice in Peosta at (563) 588-6659 or visit burdsfamilypractice.com to request an appointment. We're here for your family.

# Sick Child: Urgent Care, Doctor, or ER? | Peosta IA

URL: https://www.burdsfamilypractice.com/blog/when-should-i-take-my-sick-child-to-urgent-care-vs-the-doctor.html

← Resources & Blog
Community Health Blog

## When Should I Take My Sick Child to Urgent Care vs. the Doctor?

Published Jun 22, 2026
2 min read
By Jennifer Burds, DNP, ARNP

When your child is sick, one of the first decisions you face is where to take them. Should you call your family doctor? Head to urgent care? Go straight to the ER? It's a question we hear all the time at Burds Family Practice, and the answer depends on what's going on.
Here's a simple guide to help you decide.

### Call or Visit Your Family Doctor First (When Possible)

For most childhood illnesses, your family doctor is the best starting point. We know your child's health history, their medication allergies, their vaccination record — and we can provide follow-up care. Call us for:

- 
Ear infections, sore throats, or possible strep
- 
Pink eye
- 
Mild fevers in children over 3 months
- 
Coughs, colds, or mild respiratory symptoms
- 
Rashes that aren't spreading rapidly
- 
Well-child checkups and school physicals

### Urgent Care Is a Good Option When…

Urgent care makes sense when your doctor isn't available and the issue needs same-day attention but isn't life-threatening:

- 
Minor cuts that may need stitches
- 
Possible sprains or minor injuries
- 
UTI symptoms
- 
Vomiting or diarrhea that's moderate but manageable

### Go to the Emergency Room for These Signs

Some situations require immediate emergency care. Don't wait — go to the ER or call 911 if your child has:

- 
Difficulty breathing or turning blue
- 
A seizure
- 
Loss of consciousness
- 
Severe allergic reaction (swelling of face/throat, difficulty swallowing)
- 
Fever in a baby under 3 months
- 
Head injury with vomiting, confusion, or loss of consciousness
- 
Suspected poisoning or ingestion of a harmful substance

### When in Doubt, Call Us

If you're not sure whether your child's symptoms are serious, call Burds Family Practice. We'd rather you call and find out it's nothing than wait on something that needs attention. We're here to help you make those calls — that's what a family practice is for.
Questions about your child's health? Call Burds Family Practice in Peosta at (563) 588-6659 or visit burdsfamilypractice.com to request an appointment. We're here for your family.

# Occupational Health for Manufacturers | Burds Family Practice Peosta, IA

← Resources & Blog
Community Health Blog

## Why Local Manufacturers Are Rethinking Their Occupational Health Partner

Published May 16, 2026
4 min read
By Jennifer Burds, DNP, ARNP

If you work in HR, safety, or operations at a manufacturing company in the Dubuque area, you already know how much your occupational health vendor affects your bottom line. When a pre-employment physical takes three weeks to schedule, that's three weeks your new hire isn't on the floor. When an injured employee can't be seen quickly, recovery is delayed and workers' comp claims drag on. When paperwork takes days, your HR team is chasing forms instead of doing their job.
There's a better way — and more local manufacturers in western Dubuque County are figuring it out: your occupational health partner doesn't need to be 30 minutes away.
At Burds Family Practice in Peosta, we work with manufacturing employers across the region to provide fast, reliable occupational health services that fit how plants actually operate. Here's why it matters — and what to look for in a partner.

#### What Manufacturing Employers Actually Need from Occupational Health

When you're running a manufacturing operation, occupational health isn't a nice-to-have. It's part of how you keep production moving. The right partner needs to deliver on five things:
1. Speed. Same-week scheduling for pre-employment physicals, DOT exams, and work injury care isn't a luxury — it's a requirement. Every delay has a cost.
2. Proximity. A 10-minute drive vs. a 40-minute drive sounds small until you multiply it across dozens of employees per year. Local matters.
3. Communication. You need a real point of contact — not a call center. Someone who knows your company, your priorities, and your shift schedule.
4. Documentation. Compliance reports, return-to-work clearances, and audit-ready paperwork need to be timely and clear. Period.
5. Flexibility. Shift workers exist. Third-shift physicals exist. A good partner accommodates that.

#### The Full Suite of Services You Should Expect

A truly comprehensive occupational health partner should handle:

- 
DOT physicals for your CDL drivers — performed by certified medical examiners
- 
Pre-employment physicals tailored to your job descriptions and physical demand levels
- 
Drug and alcohol testing — pre-employment, random, post-accident, and reasonable suspicion
- 
Work injury care with timely documentation and return-to-work coordination
- 
Audiograms for OSHA-compliant hearing conservation programs
- 
Workplace vaccinations — flu shots, Hepatitis B, Tdap, and more
- 
Workers' comp coordination with your insurance carrier
If you're piecing together two or three providers to cover all of this, you're spending unnecessary time and money on coordination that should be handled by one local partner.

#### What Local Looks Like in Practice

At Burds Family Practice, we built our occupational health program with manufacturers in mind. Our clinic in Peosta is centrally located for plants across western Dubuque County — Peosta, Dubuque, Asbury, Cascade, Farley, Bankston, and beyond.
When you partner with us, you get:

- 
One dedicated point of contact — not a call center, not a rotating rep
- 
Most appointments scheduled within the same week
- 
Customized service plans built around your specific compliance needs and workforce profile
- 
Timely documentation delivered to your HR and safety teams — no more chasing reports
- 
Flexible scheduling for shift workers and seasonal hiring pushes
- 
Direct relationships with your team members so they actually feel cared for, not processed
That's the difference between a vendor and a partner. And it's what your team deserves.

#### The Real Cost of the Wrong Occupational Health Vendor

Let's put numbers to it. If your current setup adds even three days of delay between hiring and a cleared start date, multiply that by the number of new hires you onboard each year. That's lost productivity, lost training time, and frustrated managers. The same math applies to work injuries — delays in care mean longer recoveries and higher costs.
A local partner who can move fast pays for itself many times over.

#### Ready to Rethink Your Occupational Health Setup?

Whether you're already working with a provider and feel like things could be better, or you're setting up an occupational health program from scratch, we'd love to talk. We start with a quick 15-minute conversation about your operation, your workforce, and your priorities — and from there, we build a service plan that actually fits.
Let's talk. Call us at (563) 588-6659 or email bfpstaff@burdsfamilypractice.com to set up a discovery conversation.
Burds Family Practice provides occupational health services for manufacturers, employers, and CDL drivers across Peosta, Dubuque, Asbury, Cascade, Farley, Bankston, and the wider western Dubuque County, Iowa region.

# Local Healthcare in Western Dubuque County | Burds Family Practice Peosta, IA

Community Health Blog

## Why You Don't Have to Drive to Dubuque for Great Healthcare Anymore

Published May 16, 2026
4 min read
By Jennifer Burds, DNP, ARNP

We get it. For a long time, if you lived in Peosta, Asbury, Cascade, Bankston, or anywhere else in western Dubuque County and needed to see a doctor, the answer was simple: get in the car and drive to Dubuque.
And honestly? That drive adds up. Between the time, the traffic, the parking, and the waiting rooms packed with people from across the region — it could turn a simple appointment into a half-day ordeal.
Here's the good news: you don't have to do that anymore.
Burds Family Practice is right here in Peosta, and we're offering the kind of comprehensive, high-quality care that used to mean a long commute. Here's why staying local is the smarter choice for you and your family.

#### 1. Your Time Is Worth Something

Think about what it actually costs to drive into Dubuque for a doctor's appointment. By the time you factor in the drive there, finding parking, waiting to be seen, and driving home, you've easily spent two to three hours on what might be a 15-minute visit.
At Burds Family Practice, we're right in your backyard. You can pop in for a same-day appointment, actually be seen on time, and get back to your day — whether that's getting the kids from school, getting back to work, or just getting back to your life.

#### 2. Smaller Practice = More Personalized Care

Big city clinics and large health systems are busy. Really busy. That often means shorter appointments, rotating providers, and a care experience that can feel rushed and impersonal.
At Burds Family Practice, we deliberately keep our practice community-sized. That means when you call, someone who knows you answers. When you come in, your provider remembers your history, your family, and your goals. You're not starting from scratch every visit — you're continuing a relationship.
That kind of continuity isn't just more pleasant. It's actually better medicine. Providers who know you over time catch things that get missed in one-off visits.

#### 3. We Offer More Than You Might Expect

One of the biggest reasons people drive to larger cities is the assumption that more services are available there. And while that's true for highly specialized procedures, the everyday healthcare that most families need? We've got it right here.
At Burds Family Practice, we offer:

- 
Primary Care for all ages — from newborns to seniors
- 
Direct Primary Care (DPC) — a membership model with unlimited visits and direct access to your provider
- 
Occupational Health — keeping workers and employers across the area covered
- 
Medical Weight Loss — including semaglutide (Wegovy) and tirzepatide (Zepbound)
- 
Infrared Sauna Therapy — for recovery, relaxation, and overall wellness
- 
Medical Aesthetics — through SkinRx by Burds Family Practice
For the vast majority of what you and your family need, it's all right here in Peosta.

#### 4. Local Providers Are Invested in This Community

There's a real difference between a provider who commutes to a clinic and one who actually lives and works in this community. Jenny Burds didn't open a practice in Peosta by accident — she chose this community because she believes in it.
When you see a local provider, you're supporting a business that sponsors local events, hires local staff, and genuinely cares about the health of your neighbors. That investment goes both ways.

#### 5. Easier to Stay Consistent with Your Care

One of the biggest barriers to good health isn't access to a great doctor — it's the friction of actually getting there. When care is close, convenient, and relationship-based, people are more likely to keep their appointments, follow up when something feels off, and stay on top of preventive care.
That consistency is one of the most powerful things you can do for your long-term health. And it's a lot easier when your provider is 10 minutes away instead of 40.

#### When Should You Still Go to the City?

We believe in being honest with our patients. There are absolutely times when heading to a larger facility makes sense — major surgeries, highly specialized specialists, emergency trauma care. We'll always refer you to the right place when you need a level of care beyond what we provide.
But for your everyday health needs, your annual physicals, your chronic condition management, your kids' check-ups, your weight loss journey, and your wellness goals? You've got everything you need right here.

#### Come See Us in Peosta

We're proud to be the healthcare home for families across western Dubuque County — Peosta, Asbury, Cascade, Farley, Bankston, and beyond. If you've been putting off finding a local provider, let this be the nudge you needed.
Call us at (563) 588-6659, visit us at 8411 Peosta Commercial Ct Suite #8, Peosta, IA, or book online at burdsfamilypractice.com. We're accepting new patients and would love to welcome your family.
Burds Family Practice serves patients in Peosta, Asbury, Cascade, Farley, Bankston, and surrounding communities in western Dubuque County, Iowa.
